subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN OPEN SEASON ON DUCKS, GEESE AND SNIPE IN THE YUKON TERRITORY

speechtext:
Mr. GEORGE BLACK (Yukon) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 5, to amend the Migratory Birds Convention Act.
He said:	This bill consists of a short
amendment to the Migratory Birds Convention Act. Under the act as it stands, the closed season on the migratory birds mentioned in the amendment is in force until September 1. It is proposed to have the open season commence on August 15.
These migratory birds, such as ducks, geese and snipe, begin to migrate from the Yukon around the first of August and are practically all gone by September 1. The result of the present provision is that the sportsmen of the Yukon are practically prohibited from shooting these birds.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT AS TO PRESENT POSITION

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. HANSON (Leader of the Opposition) :
subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT AS TO PRESENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in my view, in the view of many hon. members of this house, and I feel quite certain in the view of many people in Canada, the war situation in Europe is more serious to-day than at any time since the fall of France. The virtual destruction of the cities of Birmingham, Bristol and Southampton, the loss of shipping as_ evidenced by press reports, and in particular the utterances of the Marquess of Lothian, his majesty's representative in the United States, particularly with respect to finance, indicate the seriousness of the position. Therefore in my view the Prime Minister should make a statement to the house and the country, if not to-day then not later than to-morrow, and tell the country just what the exact position is; because it will be understood that he has access to information which we have not. Let him tell the house and the country how serious the position is or, if we are wrong in our views, how good the position is; and especially I would request him to indicate what further, if anything, Canada can do at this juncture towards aid and assistance, whether it be in men, materials, supplies or equipment.
I am very serious about this, Mr. Speaker, and I ask the Prime Minister to give consideration to it. I do not expect him to make an immediate response, but I do feel that the situation to-day in the theatre of war over there is just as serious as it was at the time of the fall of France, and we are all very uneasy about it. I do not wish to be taken as an alarmist. The situation may not be as bad as I feel it is, but at any rate a statement from the Prime Minister would have a quieting effect upon the people at this time.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT AS TO PRESENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would say to my hon. friend that I have had in mind making a statement to the house before adjournment with respect to the situation. I should like to have a little time to think over what it would be best to say. I agree with my hon. friend in his view that the situation is a serious one. I think anyone reading the press would gather that opinion.
I would also say that such information as the government itself is receiving the press would appear to be reflecting accurately. Any statement that I may have to make will be practically in accord with what has already appeared in the press.
I may have something to say to-morrow about further proceedings before we adjourn.

speechtext:
I had intended when the motion came before the house to give hon. members the reasons for fixing as I did the 17th of February as the date for reconvening. It may perhaps not be out of place if I say just a word at the moment because in the minds of some there may appear to be reason for believing that the government is unduly delaying the time of reconvening.
I would point out first of all that two or three ministers will be absent from Canada during the month of December. The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) will be in Britain throughout the month of December. The Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) also will be going to England for the purpose of conferences with the British government. I assume it will be some time in January before he will be able to be back in Ottawa.
The conferences that will be held in London by the Minister of National Defence and the Minister of Munitions and Supply with different members of the British government will be important conferences, and legislation which may be introduced later, certainly the appropriation bill and the estimates, will in some measure be based upon the information obtained at that time.
I would also remind the house that the Christmas and New Year recess comes within the period of adjournment. That is a time when it is usually difficult to have all members of the cabinet together to discuss important matters. After continuous sittings that have lasted only a month there will 'be many matters held over pending adjournment which will require the special attention of ministers and of the cabinet before the ministers disperse even for a day or two at the Christmas season.
With respect to the conference with the provinces, the government has had to take into account and naturally would wish to consult the convenience of the different provinces, and the date fixed for the conference, the middle of January, was the earliest

Defence of Canada Regulations
that could be arranged having in mind the views expressed by some of the provinces as to a date that would be convenient to them.
I cannot say how long the conference will last, but it may be advisable not to try to conclude its proceedings too hurriedly, but rather to allow plenty of time in order that some phases at least of the report may receive detailed consideration, if there is not time for consideration of all phases. I should think that the government would be wise in keeping the last fortnight of January pretty largely for matters pertaining to the dqminion-provincial conference.
That leaves the month of February. It is true that I fixed the 17th as the date, but the 17th is a Monday. If we were calling a new session it would be called to meet on the Thursday, which would be the 13th. A fortnight will leave the government little enough time to confer after the conference with regard to the many matters that we wish to conclude before parliament reassembles and to bring before the house when it meets. Experience has taught me that it is better to have an extra week by way of preparation than to assemble at an earlier date and be running a little bit behind all the way with proceedings thereafter. I have tried to shape matters in a way that I thought would both before and after parliament reassembles best suit the convenience of members as a whole.
I might say that I gave notice when I did as to the probable time of reassembling because many members had inquired of me how long it would be after the conference before parliament would be reassembling. I thought that the sooner members generally could be advised as to the date, the better it would suit their convenience. I would also remind hon. members that we are not yet through this portion of the session. We have not reached the end of the debate on the address, and there are one or two matters, of which I shall have a word or two to say to-morrow, which will require further time and attention on the part of hon. members.

speechtext: The house resumed from Wednesday, November 27, consideraion of the motion of Mr. Brooke Claxton for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury) and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Blaekmore.

speakeroldname: Hon. N. A. McLARTY (Minister of Labour):
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe I shall best meet the wishes of this house if in the statement which I am going to give this afternoon I refrain from dealing with all aspects of the labour situation, but deal only with those that are definitely related to our war effort.
The importance of the part which labour plays in production of war materials and equipment in a mechanized war was so well expressed by the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) in this house a week ago that it is unnecessary for me to repeat it. He pointed out the accelerated tempo of productive activity now existing in this country, and explained that that tempo will increase until, in the period which he estimated at eight months, the maximum of our productive activity will have been attained. The point at which that maximum is so attained and the limitations by which it is restricted will doubtless be determined largely by the availability of labour. For that reason the problem of labour supply is a vital factor in our war achievement.
It will, of course, 'be recognized that there are necessarily limitations to the productive capacity of any country comprising twelve million people, but within that maximum limitation it is our duty to ensure the very greatest possible production and to develop
our man-power capacity to the maximum degree of efficiency. This war imposes that definite imperative. It should, too, be borne in mind and appreciated that when we reach that high point in our production so envisaged we would be producing as much, per capita, as any other country in the world.
I know that it is unnecessary to deal with many matters which are as well understood and appreciated by members of this house as by myself. It is needless, for instance, to deal with the matter of the various problems which must arise from turning our country from a peace to a war basis and developing the economic participation which war necessarily entails.
In addition, I do not have to remind this house that prior to the war we were emerging from the world's greatest depression, accompanied by the unfortunate incidence which such a depression brings, not alone on the efficiency of labour generally but peculiarly upon skilled labour as well.
Labour in general in depression times loses some of its skill; it has not the same incentive; it becomes blunt; and in addition many of our highly skilled workers returned to the United Kingdom where they felt a wider field of opportunity was open to the particular skill which they enjoyed.
Nor will I deal to-day with a strange phenomenon, namely, that notwithstanding the increased industrial activity there are still, according to the latest available figures, 52,500 employables receiving unemployment aid, to which figure must be added those unemployed who are not in receipt of relief. The degree of employability of those employables receiving unemployment aid must be seriously questioned, but notwithstanding that the paradox exists.
A similar situation exists in the United Kingdom, and the paradox has been referred to by Sir William Beveridge, chairman of the advisory committee on unemployment insurance, and explained in the following words:
The explanation of this paradox of mass overwork and mass idleness in war time is not far to seek. War, while it abolishes some types of peace-time unemployment, such as that due to cyclical depression, enormously increases another type. This is the qualitative unemployment due to the labour demanded being of one kind while the supply available is of another kind. War adds a new type of unemployment which may be described as bottle-neck unemployment, arising from the fact that the demand for labour is never a demand for labour alone, but for labour in conjunction with particular machines and particular raw materials.

The Address-Mr. McLarty

This statement of Sir William Beveridge, too, explains the circumstance that in June of this year there were in Great Britain, when the maximum of war effort was admittedly being put forth, 800,000 unemployed registered.
This paradox of unwilling idleness of many citizens in the midst of the great demands in war is surprising, 'but it is a definite fact. Bad in itself as a waste of strength, it is even worse psychologically, as suggesting to those who are being urged to additional efforts and sacrifices that these cannot really be required.
But the cure of unemployment in war is not as easy as the statement that it exists. It raises technical problems of great complexity; it involves necessarily the intimate cooperation of service and supply departments and the ministry of war services and of the ministry of labour and of the educational authorities; the organization of man-power is in the last resort a replanning and reorganizing of our whole production. The state is compelled to exert a dynamic control in the interests of the community and with the supreme object of maximum production of war requirements.
The fact, therefore, that we still have unemployed in Canada does not mean that we can face the future with complacency. Our margin of reserve of skilled and semiskilled labour is growing steadily less; and our returns of unemployment among members of trade unions show that in this class there exists the lowest unemployment figure in many years; it stands to-day at 4-4 per cent. In addition, unemployed registered at employment offices and suitable for employment in industrial war work has gradually decreased from a total of 25,500 on July 15 to 19,443 on October 15.
Taking the skilled trades alone, we find that during the same period the number of those available decreased from 11,767 to 6,345, a decrease of nearly 50 per cent. In the metal trades alone in this larger group we find a decrease from a total of 6,361 available in July to 2,950 available in October, a decline of nearly 55 per cent in this important available labour supply for industry.
I do not suggest that there is existing at present a general shortage of labour. There is not. But I do suggest there are certain specialized branches of labour in which this shortage to-day exists and which, unless adequate measures are taken to deal with its growth, will produce a situation and create a condition which will be extremely difficult to meet.

Having endeavoured to paint a reasonably fair and accurate picture of the situation as it affects labour supply, there are only two observations I desire to make:
1.	While the shortage of labour generally is not yet acute, a shortage of tool and die makers and mechanics generally is imminent, if not already at hand in some occupations.
2.	In the second place I would point out that two methods are being followed to ensure the maximum use of available labour and the training of additional skilled labour: the first is by governmental action; the second is by industry itself.
Referring to the first, governmental action, it will not be necessary in this connection to deal with the circumstances existing prior to the last session of parliament. For this reason I will not discuss the work of the dominion-provincial conference which was held shortly after the outbreak of war, the purpose of which was to secure an effective registration of skilled and semi-skilled labour available to our war industries. This resulted in a list of over 30,000 of our citizens being prepared, and this list has been kept up to date and is at present available.
Nor is it necessary for me to deal with the supply of professional technicians, a canvass of which was originally initiated by the Department of National Defence, and was undertaken by the Engineering Institute of Canada, the Canadian Institute of Chemistry, the Canadian Institute of Mining and Metallurgy, and various other professional institutes. The result of the canvass so made by these societies was later made available to the government through the work which was undertaken by Doctor Tory, and thereby over
15,000	names were made available in the technical section and afforded a reservoir of the highest skill in this highly important branch of war industry. Over 2,500 of these technicians have been referred to employers in answer to requests, and many more of them have been utilized in positions where their ability and training will be used to the best advantage.
The general problem of labour supply resolves itself into three parts:
1.	What has been done.
2.	What is being done.
3.	What it is proposed to do.
I would first like to tell the house what this government has done in connection with the basic training and development of expert labour during this war.
Through an expansion and redirection of the youth training programme and through

The Address-Mr,. McLarty
the use of funds voted by parliament for that particular programme, and drawing upon the war appropriation, the energies and work of this branch of the Labour department were all developed to the end of promoting our war work from the outset. During this past summer every one of the sixty-four technical schools in Canada possessing the required equipment and the necessary instructors was utilized for the purpose of promoting the training in war work of the young people of this country.
To-day our annual rate of training is in excess of 26,000 trainees per year, and this number is being constantly augmented and increased.
In the four months' training, which is the average time afforded, young men of this country are being given an education which will form the basis of the technical work which they are called upon to perform. The training so provided comes under two main categories:
1.	The training which is being done in the aircraft mechanics' course for entry into the Royal Canadian Air Force will develop 6,000 trainees per year at the present rate of training.
2.	The training for work in the war industries will produce an additional 24,000 basically trained workers per year.
We are, of course, hopeful of exceeding this objective, and every effort is being made I believe to bring this about.
This programme has been and is being carried out by the Department of Labour in cooperation with the various provincial governments in Canada. And might I here pay a tribute to the provincial governments for the wholehearted and loyal cooperation which they have afforded in connection with this work. It has, of course, been necessary for the dominion to increase its contribution to the carrying out of this programme.
It has, for example, given to the province concerned an additional $100 for each trainee who has completed the course in the air mechanics' class and who has been accepted by the Royal Canadian Air Force. It has been necessary also for the dominion government to absorb a substantial amount of the expense involved in the use of the vocational schools throughout Canada. But I believe that without exception the provincial governments have cooperated wholeheartedly in connection with both the air training classes and the general training of workers who will take their place in our war industries.
May I make one further remark? There are, I am advised, some of these young men
who have taken these courses and who are prepared to enter into industrial employment but are reluctant to do so because they feel that their primary duty is to join the active fighting forces of Canada on the land, on the sea and in the air. This should not necessarily be so. No inferiority complex should be created. The young man who devotes himself to industry, who endeavours to promote productive activity, who works at making bullets, is as vital and as essential as the man who fires them.
A few nights ago in the course of this debate the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Jackman) suggested that of these trainees there were approximately 25 per cent who were not placed in productive employment. Naturally his information would be based upon a certain definite time. This is a continuous thing, Mr. Speaker, and if his information were based on a certain time he might well be correct. But that is not the situation to-day. Of those who were in the summer training in our vocational schools-and I would like to make it clear to the house that that training is not limited to the summer but is going on and increasing to-day-over ninety per cent have been placed in productive activity. There are certain trainees who were trained in what might not be regarded as highly industrialized areas. It has been: necessary, and this government is paying the transportation expense to take those men from those areas which are not highly industrialized and place them in industries where they are most badly needed. And the suggestion has been definitely made to me that within the space of two weeks practically one hundred per cent of the men who have received that training will be definitely in the employment of industry.
There is too, sir, a second and very vital consideration, and that is to the extent to which industry itself has been willing to undertake and participate in the training of men for war-time industry. The duty of industry in respect of this important work was emphasized some months ago. Speaking in this house on June 17 last I pointed out that while the government might do its share in the basic training of skilled mechanics, the primary responsibility in regard to this accelerated training rested upon the shoulders of industry itself.
A canvass has been made of industry by the national labour supply council to determine the number of additional employees which will be required in carrying out the war work and the number of men which each industry is training for this purpose. While the number being trained is somewhat disappointing, there
4S4
The Address-Mr,. McLarty

is definite evidence that industry is now cooperating both with the vocational schools and in providing the necessary training in their own plants. I am confident that with this cooperation the training of workers will greatly increase during the next few months.
In addition the government has appointed and is appointing officials whose duty it is to facilitate cooperation between employers and the trainees in vocational schools, as well as to promote and increase the training being given in essential industrial plants. The work in this regard is being increased as rapidly as circumstances permit.
Might I give an instance, a rather interesting one, of an experiment which was carried on by one industry which is engaged in shipbuilding in the maritime provinces. A little time ago they placed an advertisement in fifteen newspapers, spread from Winnipeg to Calgary. The3' advertised for mechanics skilled in the manufacture of ships. The result of the advertisement was that they had applications from 227 skilled men. They selected from that number those which they required. The advice which I have received from the president of that company indicates that most of those men, who received their training in the old country, are highly skilled mechanics, I believe in the highest class of shipbuilding work, namely platens. In addition, while they are not foremen in the plants, each of these men selected is capable of training from ten to fifteen other men in the less skilled work, thereby carrying into effect a plan which will be essential if we are to keep a labour supply for our war industries. That is an example of an industry, on its own initiative, undertaking to train the necessary measure of skilled labour it requires. I believe the example might well be followed by a great many other industries in Canada; and while perhaps it is not being followed along the same line I am convinced that every war industry is endeavouring in some way to increase the volume of skilled labour available for employment.
On June 19 last the government appointed the national labour supply council, equally representative of labour and industry. That council has as its chairman Mr. Arthur J. Hills of Montreal. There are five representatives of labour and five of industry, and an equal number from each of alternate members.
This council has been extremely helpful. I have already referred to the canvass of industries which it has made to determine future labour requirements and the training being afforded by each industry. It has,

too, prepared a list of reserved occupations; and has been of assistance in maintaining in industry those workmen whose importance in industrial work is greater than it would be in the military forces. It has in addition promoted a greater mutual understanding between labour and industry.
In addition it was this council which recommended to the government that the matter of labour supply was not one with which a particular department alone was concerned, but that it required the cooperation of a number of departments. For that reason a committee of labour coordination was set up under the chairmanship of Doctor Bryce Stewart, deputy minister of labour. The other members are:
Doctor W. A. Mackintosh-Department of
Finance; Colonel George S. Currie-Department of National Defence; Major-General L. R. LaFleche-Department of National War Services; Mr. R. J. Waterous, K.C.-Department of National War Services; Mr. H. B. Chase-Department of Munitions and Supply; Mr. Arthur J. Hills-Chairman, National Labour Supply Council.

That matter, Mr. Speaker, is receiving definite attention by the committee the personnel of which I just mentioned. No doubt what action will be taken by the government will depend on certain factors. It must be remembered, for example, that in the army itself nearly forty per cent of the men have to be skilled mechanics, because of the nature of present day mechanized warfare, and I have no doubt that a fair balance will have to be maintained between those drafted into the army and those left with industry.
The duties and responsibilities of this committee are of extreme importance. It has for its general objective the determination of labour required, especially in skilled occupations, for the war effort, and the devising of ways and means of meeting these requirements. In the determination of these labour requirements, the demand from three main sources must be satisfied: the recruiting services, government agencies giving civilian employment, and firms working on government contracts. I might deal with these individually.
1.	The demand from the recruiting services, such as defence, the naval and air services, will be enlisting men. The total number of men to be enlisted during the next six months' period, the skilled occupations necessarily included and the number of men in each is being ascertained.

The Address-Mr. McLarty
2.	The demand from government agencies giving civilian employment. Men will be taken on for work in the arsenals, shipyards, the construction of airports, and other direct employment under the government. The total number and the requirements in the skilled trades for the next six months is made available to the committee by the departments concerned.
3.	The third demand, namely from government contractors and sub-contractors, is no doubt the greatest of the three. The matter of enticing of skilled labour by employers, which, if allowed to continue, would have produced a chaotic situation in industry, has already been dealt with by order in council on the recommendation of the committee. The labour needs, more especially for skilled workers, of all firms on government contracts are being ascertained and placed before the committee. These returns give the skilled occupations and the numbers required in each for the next six months or until present commitments are completed.
The data thus secured will give the committee some measurement of skilled labour requirements at present and for some months ahead and will indicate in what occupations and locations the labour is needed. This information is being supplemented by reports from all departments of government concerned. As soon as the enlistment of a quota of men, or a new governmental project or a new contract, is decided upon, the committee is to be advised so that the necessary labour may be determined and measures to secure it considered before the project is launched.
In addition this committee is engaged in the determination of the present labour reserve;' and various possible sources of labour are being canvassed to learn the number and location of required workers available.
This is being done through the following channels:
1.	Through trade unions. The unions which have members in the occupations required are being asked to furnish the committee with lists of unemployed or partially employed members or members working in non-essential industries, or men with required skills now employed in other occupations.
2.	Through the use of the provincial employment offices. The cards of the active files in the employment offices are being examined to discover applicants in the required occupations or in allied occupations, and the result of this survey is available to the committee.
3.	The same procedure as has been adopted in connection with the employment offices
will be followed in connection with the national registration cards as and when they become available.
4.	The approximate dates upon which firms can complete their commitments is being given to the committee so that new contracts may be given them without any call on the labour market, so that if new contracts are not assigned them some part of their labour force may be used elsewhere.
The committee, too, is taking steps for the conserving and augmenting of the labour supply by the following methods:
1.	In the recruiting policy they are endeavouring to ensure that men in the required occupations should not be recruited unnecessarily, and any already with the forces not being used in their trades should be returned to war industries as needed. A survey of the number of enlisted men in Canada in the scarce trades is being undertaken and the results made available to the committee.
2.	Apprenticeship. As a rule apprenticeship training covers too long a period to afford any important increase in the number of skilled workers in the emergency. Intensive instruction may speed uip the completion of courses and make a number available to industry somewhat sooner. The character of the instruction is being checked to ensure that so far as possible the men are being trained in the required occupations.
3.	Pre-employment training in technical schools, to which I have already referred. A survey is being made to ascertain that the training is being directed to the scarce trades; that it is not putting undue stress on theory; that the men are being trained in a short range of skills rather than all the skills of an occupation; that the facilities are being used in shifts in order to train the maximum number; that there is proper cooperation with local industry for use of plant equipment, and to ascertain when students <vill graduate and in what numbers.

4.	The fourth step that the committee is taking has to do with training in industry. Government contractors with proper facilities may be required to train stated numbers of workers in the scarce trades as a condition of the contract. This training should take the form of upgrading. Jobs should be broken down, and the trained mechanics should do only the most skilled part of the work. The rest of the job should be divided among a few others nearest to him in line, each of whom should be broken in on his part of the job with a few weeks' training. Others behind them should move into their places, and so on through the plant. New employees should be taken on at the lower levels and moved up as rapidly as their abilities and the circumstances permit.
A survey is being made to determine plant facilities for training in the required occupations, the instructors available and how their number may be increased, and the number of trainees that may be graduated in a given period. This survey will be first applied to war industries and then to others if deemed advisable.
5.	Training by federal government agencies. To meet their needs for skilled workers in the navy, army and air force, the arsenals and shipyards through the departments concerned must undertake to upgrade men as required of industry.

7.	A survey has been initiated to determine the number and locations of employees in the scarce trades now attached to non-essential or depressed industries who could be drawn into work on government contracts if that should become necessary.
8.	Recruiting of women for industry and war auxiliary to the services. The extent to which women may be substituted for men

The Address-Mr, McLarty
in war industries should the need arise is being studied with a view to provision for their training. As men are upgraded into higher jobs many women might be employed on jobs at the lower levels. Similarly in non-war industries, upgrading would release skilled men for war plants and, in many, women could be taken on to replace them.
9.	Labour priority for war industries. A survey is being made to establish a list of the non-essential industries which employ labour in the scarce trades and to determine the number of such workers employed. It may be found necessary to deny such industries the right to engage any additional men required in the essential occupations and, secondly, to transfer some of their skilled labour to war industries.
This gives some picture of the wide duties and functions of this committee. Its personnel is, I believe, the surest guarantee of its efficient performance of its difficult but exceedingly important task.
This brings me to another important function of this committee upon which it will have to report but which, being a matter of policy, becomes a direct responsibility of the government. We are all aware that to-day all our citizens are called upon to make sacrifices-sacrifices which will be all the greater as the war progresses and time marches on. This is a total war, and the primary duty of government in the matter of sacrifice is to see that it is equally distributed.
Many will plead that they are making more sacrifices than their neighbours. But our world to-day is inspired by those who bear their heavy griefs with patience; it pays little heed to those who parade their petty grievances with impatience.
In Canada to-day our war effort depends on two great services-our fighting services and our producing services. Each is essential, each is interdependent, and each is determined to back the other to the utmost degree. But maximum production depends on the most efficient possible use of the human and material resources at our disposal. Manufacturing plants must be well equipped with modern tools and machinery and skilled men and women. They must operate to capacity within the limits of sustained efficiency. Wherever possible they must operate on two or even three shifts and in many instances production is continuous so that operation subject to another day being finished even on Sunday is necessary.
These conditions do not obtain generally in peace time, and it is but natural that the transition to war-time conditions raises problems concerning relations between employer and
employee, principally the problem of remuneration for work done. In peace time, when the supply of labour has been plentiful, the tendency has been towards a shorter day and working week. That purpose has been twofold ; originally to reduce fatigue and provide leisure for recreation; and later to spread the work and reduce unemployment.
The working day has been reduced to eight hours generally and the week to forty-four hours. Provision exists for the working of hours in excess of those outlined above, under special conditions, and overtime rates of pay have been established. These rates usually provide for payment of rates fifty per cent higher than straight time and in the case of work performed on Sundays, one hundred per cent higher. These last are punitive rates, designed to discourage the working of a seven day week. We must now give careful consideration to the question of the application of such punitive rates when war conditions have practically eliminated the reasons which originally necessitated their introduction. In the case of work which has to be performed on Sundays, some employees will be so employed but if they* are given another day off during the week instead, it would be hard to defend the payment of punitive rates for Sunday work.
To-day we are approaching the point where, even generally speaking, a labour shortage will exist, and under the circumstances we must consider the question of lengthening the standard working week from forty-four hours to forty-eight or even higher, as the new basis for calculating what overtime rates shall be payable. We have reached the point at which, instead of planning to spread the work, we are actually seeking workers to man our rapidly expanding war industries.
With the distressing news concerning havoc wrought by the enemy in such centres as Coventry, Birmingham, Bristol and Southampton still ringing in our ears, and with the Minister of Shipping admitting that sinkings are going on at a greater rate than replacements, I suggest that this is no time for us to be thinking of maintaining standards which do not take into account the urgency of the situation.
In considering the possibility of lengthening the working week we appreciate that this involves the possible temporary-I should like to emphasize that, Mr. Speaker-the temporary relinquishing of certain standards which labour has established over the years. The only excuse for asking that these temporary concessions-and it must be admitted that they are temporary and for the emergency period only-be considered is that we must win the war, and sacrifice is unavoidable.

I can answer that quite readily. In the order in council passed by this government on June 19, in which we made certain observations as to what we considered was the best method of preserving the best possible relations between industry and labour in war time, we made it very clear that any concession made by labour in this emergency period would be for the emergency only. In his address a couple of weeks ago to this house the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) reinforced that statement of policy by stating that when labour was making these concessions it was our definite duty when the emergency was over to see that labour did not suffer as a result. I do not think there can be any question about this government's attitude.
If lengthened, the working week must not be made inordinately long, as experience has taught us that beyond certain limits, fatigue more than offsets any advantage gained in production as a result of longer hours. The present working week is short of the point at which fatigue becomes a factor, and it may be found desirable to lengthen progressively the working week as the available labour supply diminishes.
Should these steps be found desirable, the sacrifice involved will be offset to a very large extent by increased incomes due to steady work and longer working hours, and by the controls 
adopted which have effectively protected all from unduly increased living costs. A study of workers' incomes in certain industries reveals the fact that where wage increases have been ten per cent since the outbreak of war, actual incomes have increased much more, and I suggest therefore that it is a problem of adjusting labour standards in the war effort by rational and logical approach on the part of all concerned.
The interest of the public in the situation is a very definite one indeed, exceeding in some cases the interest of the employer. This interest is, of course, evident from the fact that the government is the principal buyer, and in addition because of the policy which the government has followed to prevent the exploitation of war-time needs by any form of profiteering. One of the means to this end adopted by the government was to require all those who tender on government orders to do so on the basis of existing prices for labour and material, the government undertaking in some instances to protect the contractor against increases in either labour or material. This has saved the taxpayers of Canada a considerable amount of money.
I should like to put on Hansard-l am reminded of it by the question of the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis)- one or two resolutions to show the attitude of labour and the cooperative viewpoint that now exists. Here is a resolution from a group of working men which indicates clearly their attitude of cooperation and willingness to accept their share of sacrifice in making common cause against the enemy. It is from the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers in Toronto, and reads:
That we notify all employers of our members we have decided to temporarily suspend the provision of our now existing agreement, which limits the hours of work, and will work eight hours per day, six days per week at straight time, during the present crisis, these to be between the hours of 8 a.m. and 5 p.m. on Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday and Saturday (holidays not included). It being distinctly understood that our agreement, as at present constituted, shall remain unchanged and the suspended provision shall immediately, at the end of this crisis, automatically become effective.
A few days ago a friend of mine was talking to the general manager of a large industrial plant. He asked the general manager if they were experiencing any difficulty in stepping up their production. The general manager replied that they were not. They called a meeting with their employees, told them the facts of the situation, and asked for suggestions. The outcome was a voluntary
4S9

The Address-Mr. Homuth
arrangement whereby employees in that plant are working at more than prescribed hours per week for straight time wages.
I could give a great many examples, Mr. Speaker, of plants in which the same thing is happening. But the point is, when it is suggested that this be done by some arbitrary method, that the best way to do it is by mutual local agreement, and this method has been followed in a great many instances.
I have here another resolution passed by the carpenters' union of the city of Regina:
Therefore be it resolved that we, the carpenters of Regina, represented by the above mentioned local union, do hereby promise, from this date and until this present war is won by the British empire of which we are proud to be a part, "to work on government war work only for straight time for ten hours each day and for six days per week, including Sundays and holidays, for the rate of wages as set out in the agreement and signed by all parties concerned" for all carpenters and for all carpenter work.
I merely give these, sir, as typical illustrations of the willingness of labour to cooperate voluntarily.
There is, sir, a right way and a wrong way to deal with and adjust every problem of human relations. It has been urged upon the government that by some fiat, by some ukase, we should order labour to do certain things in the matter of wages paid or hours of labour worked. There might be conceived some circumstances in which the government might be required to take such action. But those circumstances do not exist to-day. What labour is looking for is not regimentation but direction. It has made that abundantly clear. Dealing as we are with a cooperative body, why should such action be necessary? That is the wrong way.
I was interested in reading a report of the remarks made by the Minister of Labour in Great Britain, in the House of Commons yesterday, in which he said:
Had we applied conscription of labour in the manner suggested, we should have made direct for defeat. Compulsion does not give the desired result.
The right way is to assume that this is fundamentally labour's war, and that being so, that labour-organized and unorganized- is willing to contribute its maximum effort in this critical time. It involves a definite consultation with labour, a testing-out of the viewpoint of labour. The use of the big stick is unnecessary when we are all engaged in a common purpose. I am convinced that that is the right way. And I am equally convinced that if we adopt it, it will redound to the benefit of the Canadian people during war time, it will be of definite assistance in 14873-32
the aftermath of war, and it will immeasurably promote the happiness and prosperity of our Canadian people.

Mr. KARL K. HOMUTH (Waterloo South): First, I want to congratulate the Minister of Labour (Mr. McLarty) on a very enlightening address to this house. An address like that is the sort of information which this house wants from the ministers who have the responsibility of carrying on our war effort.
I wish also to congratulate you, Mr. Speaker, on the attitude you have taken with respect to the reading of speeches in this chamber. I would hesitate to interrupt a speaker who is reading a speech, to draw the fact to your attention, but on several occasions I have spoken to you personally,

The Address-Mr. Homuth

because I do feel the practice is unfair. In my opinion the same rule should apply to cabinet ministers. I say that in fairness to the private members of this house. Cabinet ministers should not be accorded any more consideration, except on occasions when, for example, they are making some statement which deals with a new policy, or dealing with some matter of international importance, or reading exhaustive figures. I congratulate you, Mr. Speaker, upon your attitude in this respect, although I think that, as regards new members-and we can leave this to your judgment'-they should be given more leeway in their maiden speeches than those who have been in the house for some time and have previously taken part in its debates.
Before I enter upon the general subject matter of my remarks, I feel constrained to make emphatic reference to something which has happened in the last two or three days. I refer to the decision announced by the board of governors of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to defer action against the Transradio press service. To my mind this is a serious matter. A few days ago the Dies committee in the United States issued a white paper in which they showed that this service received some $44,000 for the purpose of broadcasting nazi propaganda throughout Canada and the United States. It was as a result of this disclosure that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation's governors decided to appoint a committee and take action. I believe they have now referred it to a subcommittee. I am sorry that they have not taken definite action and ruled these people off the air. We have enough to contend with in this country without having that insidious nazi propaganda going over the airways of Canada, and I hope that the minister will decide to take definite action in this matter. It is a serious thing. Propaganda of this kind can do a great deal of harm to our war effort.
There is no one who would at any time question the courage of the men in our army, our air force, and our navy. The fact that they are in the service is sufficient evidence of their courage. But we must have courage in other places in this country. We must have courage in this house. We must have courage in this government,-courage to do the things which are necessary to the war effort, courage to pass such laws as are necessary to give the greatest help we can to the mother country in this hour of extreme peril. I feel that sometimes we are inclined to soft-pedal some of our responsibilities because of some political effect that action might have on portions of our population. That thing must not be. Here in this 
house, and particularly with the ministers, there must be courage to face these issues as we have never faced issues before.
I have heard during this debate rather alarming things from some hon. members. Two or three, for example, have referred to an undergrading of wheat going to the elevators in western Canada. For many years I have heard these charges; I do not know whether they are true or not, but statements to this effect have been made on the floor of the house. It is a serious matter. Goodness knows the farmer gets little enough for the products he raises. If undergrading is going on, the government should have the courage to have it stopped and to see to it that wherever cases of the kind can be traced, farmers are reimbursed for anything out of which they have been cheated.
The hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Esling) made the statement yesterday that many of the British Columbia Doukhobors have not registered, that they defy our laws. There can be no neutrality in Canada in regard to the war. We are either for our war effort or against it. If there are in any community in this country people who are not prepared to play their part, this government and the authorities must take action against them. Any man in my district who failed to register-and there have been a few-has been taken into court and fined, or, if he cannot pay the fine, he must go to gaol. They tell me that some of these people would be glad to go to gaol. Well, perhaps gaol is too good for them. If so, they should be put in an internment camp and made to work. At any rate, they should be compelled to live up to the laws of Canada. These are some of the things in which we must show courage, particularly at a time such as this.
The other day I was amazed when the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) raised a question with reference to the men who had been arrested at the Chrysler plant and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) stated that it was under an order in council passed by the government that this plant had been declared a protected area. The hon. member for Cape Breton South inquired whether the Department of Justice had ordered the arrest of these strikers, and the reply of the Minister of Labour was:
My information is that the arrests were made by local and provincial police, under the instructions, not of the dominion government but of the Attorney General of Ontario.
These men were arrested because of the violation of a law passed by this House of Commons. The police officers, whether they

The Address-Mr. Homuth
be municipal, provincial or federal, are sworn to uphold the law. This law is our responsibility ; it was passed by the government of the day. It was under this law that these men were arrested. Let us, then, take responsibility for it. Let us show that we have the courage to stand by the things which we believe are necessary in our war effort.
I have been particularly pleased during this session to listen to the tolerant speeches which have been made. Only on one or two occasions have there been speeches that savoured perhaps of politics. I do wish however to associate myself with the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) in his mild, yet, I think, deserved criticism of the government or of some members of the government wYho, when we offer certain criticisms of the government, are inclined to yell something across the floor of the house to the effect that we are sabotaging the war effort. I realize it only comes from two or three sources, but it is rather unkind, because there is not a member of this house who is not definitely behind the government in everything it is willing to do in this war effort.
I wish to refer for a moment to one-third of the speech made by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner). I have a very high regard for the Minister of Agriculture. No one loves a political battle more than I do; no one will fight any political battle harder than I will; and I like to hear the Minister of Agriculture, at other times than the present at any rate, when he is making very strong fighting speeches. I say, I like to hear him, and therefore often, when we have dented the armour of the government, I have watched private members turn their faces pleadingly to the Minister of Agriculture, waiting for the moment when he will get up and rescue the government from the criticisms of the opposition.
The Minister of Agriculture referred to the election of March 26 and rather prided himself on winning his riding and on the fact that the government had come back with such a large majority. Perhaps we are all willing to admit that at that time the war efforts of this government were considerably beclouded-*

Were
there any?

speechtext:
Of course, what there
were. But later on in the following session a certain truth came out that more or less substantiated the stand we had taken. The people of the country are not interested in political speeches; they do not want political speeches. We are at war. Let us therefore fight our political battles when the proper time 14873-324
comes, but while we are at war, let us show that tolerance that has been so prevalent throughout this session, and let everyone do his utmost to further our war effort.
There are rumours. We all hear rumours, rumours that are sometimes disturbing, and in my opinion if the government were a little more frank with the people many of these rumours would disappear. Greater frankness will dispel these rumours, and that is one thing we must make sure of. I have listened carefully to the minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston), the Minister of National Defence for Air (Mr. Power), the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services (Mr. Macdonald) and the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe). One of the unfortunate things I find-and it is more prevalent in some departments of government-is that we still have our peace-time set-up, and our peace-time set-up is not good enough. Some of these men cannot adapt themselves to the war-time tempo and when problems arise which the minister feels perhaps are too much for him to handle he creates another board. Board after board has been set up in Canada and I doubt whether a member of the cabinet can get up and tell us how many boards there are operating in	the city	of	Ottawa	andthroughout the country. The question is: Are these boards	coordinating	their efforts,
and are they doing the job they are intended to do? How many of these boards are clashing with each other in the work they have to carry out?
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) the other day told us of the great need for money. We all agree with him. There is an old saying that if you take	care of	the	pennies	thepounds will take	care of	themselves.	We
have wasted a lot of money in this war effort, and I say this not in any spirit of criticism. What I have to say to-day is said entirely because I wish to assist in every way I can and to help the government in its war effort. But we have wasted a lot of money because we have retained for many months the peacetime set-up which was disastrous to the work we had to do in preparing for this war. At the beginning of the war-and to some extent this is still taking place-goods manufactured hundreds of miles from Ottawa were shipped into Ottawa for inspection and shipped back to the very town or city from which they came, to be distributed to the troops. I have seen cloth from a mill hundreds of miles from this city sent 'here for inspection and shipped back to within two blocks of the mill to be made into overcoats. It was the peacetime set-up that was the cause of the waste of so much money. I say to the government that if they would look into many of these
The Address-Mr. Homuth

smaller things they could save far more money than they are getting in from their war savings stamps.
I have seen ten trucks waiting at the freight shed to take a load a distance of half a mile, and they took two loads in a day when two trucks could have taken ten loads in the day. These are things for practical men to deal with, men who have the ability to organize, and they could be the means of great savings to this government.
The people are being taxed as they were never taxed before, and what they are being taxed to-day will be almost nothing in comparison with what they will have to pay in the future. They are not complaining, and they are not going to complain, but they do ask whether the government is getting a dollar of value for every dollar spent. In so many areas they have seen such waste of money that they become a little suspicious of our war effort.
The Minister of National Defence spoke of the building of barracks. I have no hesitation in saying that was one of the most extravagant jobs ever carried on in this country. By letting the contracts to local contractors, who would have bid on them and put them up in just as quick time, there would have been a saving of hundreds of thousands of dollars. But the army went ahead and built these things and the carelessness and waste of money and time was enormous. I say to the government that this peace-time organization is no good. Get the best men you can get. particularly practical men, men who know something about these jobs, not men who have sat behind mahogany desks in offices but superintendents of plants, builders and men who can be very useful to this government and are only too anxious to be so.
For the first time in the history of this country, I suppose, we had a civilian as master of the ordnance. On several occasions I went to see him with certain suggestions which I thought would save the government money and also save foreign exchange. I never knew a man in a government office more responsive to suggestions. than Mr. Chester was. Sometimes within a week the new order went out and the change was made, meaning an immense saving to the government. Now I understand Mr. Chester is leaving, and I think a newspaper man is coming to take his place. Mr. Chester is a practical man; I am sorry he is going. I believe that those of us who have had associations with him, who know of his ability and what he was able to accomplish. are entitled to an explanation from the Minister of National Defence as to why that man is leaving the service of the country.
Mr. Homuth.]
Now for a moment I should like to deal with finance, and particularly with the last war loan. I was very much interested in what the Minister of Finance said the other day. But I do believe, as my leader and other members of this house believe, that the last war loan was not the success it ought to have been, in spite of the fact that we may have received thirty or forty million dollars more than we asked for. We did not get the money from the sources to which we were appealing. I believe that right in the middle of it the government changed its mind as to its policy in raising money. Prior to the war loan being advertised prominent men from one end of this country to the other received a telegram from this government asking if they would cooperate and organize for the purpose of selling the war loan. I venture to say that in every instance the government got a reply expressing every willingness to cooperate, just as men were willing to cooperate in the last war. But that was the last these men ever heard of it. They were never called into conference; they were never asked to get together and organize. Apparently after sending out the wires the government decided to sell the war loan through the brokerage houses. So that in every village and town and city in this country every insurance agent, anyone at all who knew a brokerage house, could write in and ask for the privilege of selling the bonds. There was no enthusiasm stirred up; there was no local committee, nothing done to encourage the people, particularly those with the smaller savings in the banks, to participate in this loan.
I hope that when subscriptions to the next war loan are being asked from the people of this country the government will go back to the system we had in the last war, when nrominent men throughout the country held public meetings, stirred up enthusiasm, brought home to the people their responsibility to subscribe; also that it will be in such denominations that people can buy S50 and $100 worth, as they did in the last war, and that they shall be able to get them through the offices of the industries with which they work.

speechtext: And get six per cent.

speechtext:
My hon. friend says six per cent. I am sick and tired of hearing about the percentage being paid on the war loan. I have enough confidence in the people ot this country to feel sure that if they have to lend their money for nothing they will do it, if only we give them the leadership.
Another suggestion I want to make to the Minister of Finance and the Minister ot

The Address-Mr. Homuth
National War Services is in respect to our Red Cross and allied services. In our town-*
I think we were the first town in the country to do it-we put on a joint drive last year. We assured the people of our municipality that they would be asked only once in the year to subscribe to these various war services. We linked the Red Cross, the Salvation Army, the Knights of Columbus, the Y.M.C.A. and local requirements all together. Our people, knowing that they were not going to be asked to subscribe to some different service every two or three months, contributed exceptionally well, oversubscribed what we asked for, and thus we were able to take care of our allotment for all these various services. The government should give leadership in seeing that that same thing is done throughout this whole country. It has worked exceptionally well, and many municipalities are taking it up. Why the Red Cross object to it I do not know, but I understand there is an objection. It has worked well, and people subscribed freely; whereas if you make four or five appeals in a year they get tired of the continuous pleading for money. I suggest that the government give leadership in this matter.
I thought perhaps this afternoon the Minister of Labour would make some reference to what was said by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) in his broadcast a week ago last Sunday night. I thought perhaps the Minister of Munitions and Supply would make some reference to it. Apparently this famous master mind from Saskatchewan, who spent most of his life on a farm or teaching school, tells his fellow ministers, the heads of industry in this country and the great mass of industrial workers just what should and can be done so far as trained industrial workers are concerned. He went to England; I believe he was away for six weeks. So far as he could he settled all problems with regard to wheat, pork, cheese and fruits. He did all those jobs; he did a little travelling round the country; he inspected the ruins; I believe he had an audience with his majesty. Undoubtedly he was invited out for luncheon and dinner on various occasions. 1 do not know whether he slept at all, but certainly when he returned hs gave us to understand that in the course of the time that elapsed between leaving here and returning, he had done all these things and, in addition, had become an expert on industry. He told us that industry in this dominion needed to have only five per cent of its employees skilled workmen.

speechtext:
The lone voice from Hal ton is heard again. I do say, however, that the statement the minister made was serious, and both industry and labour are wondering whether the remarks of the Minister of Agriculture represent the considered ideas of the government of the day. Men who have spent three, four or five years as apprentices; men and women who have spent two or three years learning, and then gone on for many more years before becoming absolutely efficient in their jobs, want to know if that is the attitude of the government. Is that what the government thinks of skilled labour in this country?
The Minister of Labour himself comes from a district in which there are industries employing highly skilled men, doing some of the finest work; industries in which nearly every employee is highly skilled. The Minister of Labour knows the statement of the Minister of Agriculture is not correct. Therefore I feel that before this debate is over, some member of the cabinet ought to clear the air. If the Minister of Agriculture made that statement on his own responsibility, without giving the matter adequate consideration, let him admit it. Everyone makes mistakes; we are all bound to make them, but this seems to me rather a serious mistake. I come from a highly industrialized county, and I can say that the heads of our industries have been only too willing to cooperate in every way with the Department of National War Services, and have been willing to do everything possible in order to permit their men to take military training. They feel, however, that a policy or idea such as this will be disastrous to our industrial set-up and to the tempo of industrial life in Canada.
For a moment I should like to deal with a particular activity in my own riding. I was interested in what the Minister of Labour said about the training of youth. I do not think in this country there is a youth training scheme that has done as good work as is being done at the Galt aircraft school. Here I should like to pay a tribute to the minister of labour of Ontario, who is doing a wonderful job there. As a result of his practical knowledge of industry and labour, and of this sort of work, he has built up at Galt a school
The Address-Mr. Homuth

which has turned out about 1,100 aircraft workers now employed in the aircraft factories of this dominion, as well as about 1,000 young men who have taken their places in the air force. That school started in September with 200 men. The next class numbered 300; these were for the air force only. The third class numbered 613. Every time they have been asked by the government to double the number of students they have done so, and I believe the government might ask them once more to double their number. I believe they are able to do so; I think they have the necessary instructors with which to carry on. I would suggest that the number of students be greatly increased, because this is one of the sources from which we are obtaining not only our air mechanics but also the skilled workers for the various aeroplane factories in Canada.
I am told by industrialists who have taken these boys into their plants that within three months these boys are as far advanced in machine-shop practice as an ordinary boy taking three years of instruction in a technical school. That of course is because of the intense training these boys receive. I feel that a few more of these schools throughout the country would do a great deal towards looking after the boys who are coming out of school who are too young for the army but who may be able to supply the great demand for skilled labour that is gradually becoming felt.
There is however one disquieting rumour which I have heard on more than one occasion. It is that the government has been considering the erection of a factory for the purpose of training these students. I do not know whether or not that is true; I hope the minister will tell us. I hope it is not true, because we have throughout Canada hundreds of factory buildings that could be utilized for this purpose. I feel that perhaps in our war effort we are putting into bricks and mortar too many dollars that we ought to be putting into the things we require to fight this war. I travel across this country two or three times a year, and I know something of the various industrial centres. There are those who say that it does not matter how much money we spend in our war effort; that if we lose the war, our money will be gone anyway. Well, I say it is not so much a question of how much we spend but how we spend it. We are not going to lose the war; we are going to win it, but in whatever we do now let us have some sort of planned national economy. Let us make use of the vacant factories there are down in the mari-times, in Quebec, in Ontario and throughout western Canada. We have vast quantities

of gas and coal in Alberta and in Saskatchewan, and we should make full use of all these things which are requisite to industrial production.
Instead of building Up vast industries as we are doing-I am rather fearful of the millions and tens of millions which are being put into new factories-we should spread out this work. I understand that the capitalization of these industries is to be wiped out in a period of five years. We should attempt to decentralize industry; we should spread out this w'ork through all the cities, towns and villages of this country. If that were done, we would be doing much to help our national economy when this war is over. Where there is a concentration of industry in a few centres we accentuate the housing difficulties. The first thing we know we shall be building shacks for the workers and their families to live in. If there is such a thing as war-time prosperity, how much better it would be to take this prosperity to all our cities, towns and villages. We could thus take advantage of housing and factory accommodation that is available and provide the farmer wTith a local market, which he does not get with the concentration of industry we have under the present set-up.
The minister should have given us some idea of how all these plans are working out and of just what arrangements were being made with regard to profits where an industry is already established and is being given millions of dollars with which to build additions. These are matters which we should watch very carefully. This house should be given some explanation of them, and that is why I had hoped the estimates would have been down before this. If we had this information it would not be necessary to interrupt the ministers when they are making their statements.
I appeal to the government to give hon. members and the people throughout the country an opportunity of serving in this W'ar. AVhen the government decided to hold a national registration, they came to the members of this house for help, and every member responded. They went home and did their utmost to see that the registration was carried out properly. Give us something to do, in connection with either a war loan or some other activity. There are no politics to-day. The only politics we have now is the winning of this war. When the war is won, then we can go back to the political battles we have had in the past.
We are spending $100,000,000 in this war compared with every $10,000,000 we spent in the last. This is a tremendous amount of money to be spending. Unfortunately in

The Address-Mr. Lizotte
every country there are people who, regardless of its dire need, regardless of how freedom is being threatened, are prepared to take advantage of the times and become rich at the expense of their country. There are undoubtedly some such people in Canada, and we should be very careful in making these tremendous expenditures. I have always abhorred the word " scandal," and in my political career I have never resorted to its use or to personalities of any kind. Perhaps one of the worst things that could happen in our war effort would be to have a scandal develop. I ask the ministers to do everything possible so that, whatever expenditures are made, the Canadian people will feel assured that such expenditures are being made properly and that no opportunity is being given to those vultures who are so often ready to feed at a time like this.
Nothing could be more devastating to our war effort than to have something like that happen. I am a Conservative, I believe in Conservative policies, and when the time comes I am going to fight to put my party into power. But now we are Canadians; that is the only term we should know. If any hon. member should learn of anything at all suspicious, he should go to the minister concerned and tell him the story. Then, if there is anything to the rumour, the minister will have an opportunity to clean up things. Mistakes are bound to be made, but I think that hon. members should see to it that such matters are brought to the attention of the particular minister who is responsible. It should be done quietly. These things are bound to happen and we should be most careful. I say to the government that so long as they carry on and do everything they possibly can, I am behind them and will do everything I can to assist them in their war effort.
