speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising from my seat I recall having read somewhere in the Bible-a book which has no secrets for my reverend friend the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor)-that there is a time to speak and a time to remain silent. I fear that the hon. members of this house will tell me, now that the Christmas adjournment is approaching, that this is a time for me to remain silent rather than to speak. However, seeing in front of me and around me such examples of eloquent loquacity-especially my good friend the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot)-I cannot resist the pleasure of saying at least a few words during the present debate. Besides, as the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) has said, it is proper that, as the
representative of a certain section of the population, a member of the House of Commons should give utterance to his views and those of his constituents. In keeping with my life-long habit, I shall be brief.
I cannot let this occasion go by without adding my congratulations to those which have been so justly offered to the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. Both hon. members represent a minority group in their respective provinces. Both do so with distinction. I particularly congratulate my excellent friend the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Jutras), whose truly French name is frequently encountered in the province of Quebec, on the good French accent he has retained in the English-speaking province where he lives.
During the last session, when I was a newcomer, I was somewhat struck by the morbid irritability which prevailed in this house, especially on the opposition benches. I wondered whether our parliament was always the seat of a war of nerves. I am ready to believe that the tragic events then occurring in Europe with lightning speed were to a certain extent the cause of this nervousness. Those who did not share the government's views, the members of that party which at the recently held general elections had been weighed by the people and found wanting, were loud in their cries that our war effort was worthless, that the defence of the country was poorly prepared, that the government was slumbering instead of rushing to arms and sending Canadians to do battle-they knew not where, but, anyhow, across the seas, even if England did not need them.
I was glad to see that the government was not letting itself be impressed by this rash criticism. Indeed, amid those loud cries and passionate appeals, those who presided over the destinies of the country continued to work calmly and silently, as is proper in war time, devoting all their energy to the task of ensuring the security of the Canadian people.
Today, to the utter amazement of our opponents, who can hardly credit their eyes or their ears, we are witnesses of the prodigious, indeed the miraculous effort accomplished by the government in order to provide our country with the necessary armour to fight victoriously on land, on sea and in the air, and to help Great Britain to win this war which is the war of all those who cherish their traditions, their civil and political liberties and their physical and moral existence.
I listened with deep attention to the speeches recently delivered by the Minister of National War Services (Mr. Gardiner), the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston), the Minis-
The Address-Mr. Lizotte

ter of National Defence for Air (Mr. Power), the Minister of National Defence for Naval Affairs (Mr. Macdonald), the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe), the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley), and, to-day, to the speech of the Minister of Labour (Mr. McLarty). They have given us detailed stalaments-as detailed as is possible in time of war-of the prodigious efforts put forth and the magnificent results obtained. I was satisfied and deeply impressed.
I then read their statements as recorded in Hansard, and as all those who have taken the trouble to do so, I became convinced that they had, in less than one year, written glorious pages which more advanced countries would be proud to have written in several years.
The government having put forth an effort greater, in my opinion, than our means justify, those who publicly proclaim that we have not done enough must be utterly lacking in responsibility and generosity. Our prodigious effort will continue, and glorious pages will still be written by those to whom the Canadian people have entrusted the preservation of their security, their democratic principles and their liberty.
Mr. Speaker, a question frequently brought up is that of national unity. It has been broached on many occasions in recent months and again during this session. We must never cease thinking of it. So far, in spite of our prodigious effort, in spite of the enormous sacrifices laid on the Canadian people, the national unity which the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) have striven so hard to build up has been preserved. May the government ever continue to direct its policy, to steer its course, towards that goal, that promised land of the Canadian ideal-national unity. May the government ignore threats and intimidation and carefully refrain in its war effort from moves those who hear me and will read my speech will understand what I mean-from moves capable of destroying in a single day the work of many years and the national unity which the leader of the party at present in charge of the affairs of the country has, in cooperation with the recognized leader of the province of Quebec, spent his life in building up.
The mobilization act was voted by the representatives of the province of Quebec as by those of the other provinces. We all understand, in Quebec as in the other provinces, that it is our bounden duty to defend our mothers, our wives, our children, our homes and our land. Therefore, the people of Quebec, just as the people of the other prov-[Mr. Lizotte.3
inces, have agreed willingly and even enthusiastically to lend their sons for military training for the defence of Canadian territory. They will likewise agree to give them to the country when the country will be in danger. But the people of Quebec, who are attached to their land, object to all uncalled-for zeal likely to prove unnecessarily harmful, especially to the farming class, the class which interests me most, since my constituents are mostly farmers. There is some talk of amending the regulations made under the mobilization act with a view to extending the training period from one month to four months. The members of the house will not be called upon to deal with this question, but I humbly urge upon the government to take steps to see that agriculture is not harmed and that the farmers and farmers' sons are not taken from the land where their services are required. It has been suggested that the farmers would be trained during what is called the slack season. But, Mr. Speaker, there is no such thing as a slack season of four months in farming. And should the farms be deprived of the labour required to operate them, confusion will set in and agriculture will be seriously inconvenienced.
I have sufficient confidence in my leaders and in the government which I have always supported and will continue to support to know that they will carefully consider this problem and see that this difficulty does not arise.
I fully agree with the view expressed by the hon. member for Glengarry (Mr. McDiarmid) on Tuesday last in the following words:
In my opinion food was the chief factor in the winning of the last war, and lack of food was the cause of the collapse of Germany. The food blockade of enemy countries and the production of food in the allied countries constituted one of the chief means of winning the last war, and we are all of the opinion that the same means will be responsible for victory in this war.
I am sure, therefore, that the government will not take amiss the humble suggestion of the humblest of representatives of a rural constituency. I am confident that the necessary measures will be taken to avoid harming the agricultural class and the country's food production.
Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, the people of Quebec have insisted, still insist and shall ever insist that the sacrifices they have accepted to make must be voluntary and must remain voluntary. Besides, this attitude is general throughout all the provinces of the dominion. On that condition and that condition alone will the old province of Quebec continue to give its men to the

The Address-Mr. Douglas (Weyburn)
country for the defence of Canada and voluntarily send many of its sons for service overseas, for it is a fundamental tenet of our democratic belief that freedom should be defended by free men and that it is free men who can best defend the empire which protects us and our own country, Canada, whose interests we wish to safeguard first and above all.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, owing to the fact that I was qualifying at Dundurn military camp for a commission in the Canadian Army, it was not possible for me to hear the speeches made by the mover and the seconder of the address. I have, however, read their speeches, and I want to offer to both those gentlemen my congratulations upon launching this debate on so high a plane.
My remarks will naturally divide themselves into two main themes: first, some of the problems inherent in our war effort; and, second, the need of an agricultural programme to prevent the complete economic collapse of western Canada.
The first and most pressing matter witt reference to our war effort is the lamentable shortage of essential equipment for the fighting services. No useful purpose can be served at this time by dwelling unnecessarily upon some of that lack, nor by drawing a picture which can serve only to give comfort to the enemy. Nevertheless I, with every other member of this house, have a responsibility to the men who are in the fighting services. I had the privilege for several weeks of living with some of the men who are training for the purpose of fighting in defence of freedom. I cannot speak too highly of the instructional personnel or of the morale of the young men who are being trained. But I would point out, Mr. Speaker, that excellent instructors and enthusiastic youth are not enough when men are asked to drill with obsolete Springfield rifles which cannot even be fired, when artillerymen are working with imitation guns hewn out of trees, and when many of these units have had their only contact with modern equipment consist of fleeting glimpses of a Bren gun being whisked from unit to unit and from camp to camp.
As I pointed out to the house last year, this is a delicate subject, both for the members of the opposition and for the administration. There are questions which we cannot ask in this house without arousing fears and suspicions. and, believe me, sir, that is the last thing I want to do. At the same time we fare not refrain from asking certain questions, lest we be derelict in our duty to the men whose lives may be jeopardized through lack of that equipment. That is why I asked the
government last year to consider the appointment of a committee of the house to which confidential information could be given from time to time regarding the progress made in securing equipment very much as was done in Great Britain yesterday, where a secret session of parliament was held in order to give information about the organization of the army. The government has not seen fit to comply with that request. We have, therefore, no alternative than to raise these matters on the floor of this house.
To say the very least, the supplying of war equipment has been far from satisfactory. We ought to be told, for instance, why it is that we are not in production of the Lee-Enfield rifle in the Dominion of Canada. We are told that we shall be in production in 1941-which means that by the time we have been at war for a year and a half or two years we shall be producing that most elementary of all weapons, the infantry rifle.
This house has a right to know when we shall b.e in production of anti-tank guns. I am told by those who are in a position to know, that the anti-tank rifles with which Canadian troops are now being trained are about as effective as pea-shooters and as obsolete as the bow and arrow. When do we expect to be producing an effective anti-tank gun, and in what quantity?
We should be told what steps are being taken by the government to produce Bren light machine guns in other plants than the John Inglis factory-either in other private plants, or in government arsenals, as the British are doing in the Woolwich arsenal. From time to time glowing reports have been given to the effect that the production of the Bren machine gun was far ahead of schedule. But until recently it has been almost impossible to get figures. The other day the minister gave them to the press, but not to the house. The statement is that we are to have 1,750 light Bren machine guns by next March. May I remind the house that the contract which was drawn up with the John Inglis plant in 1937 called for 1,000 light machine guns by the 1st of April, 1941. But the government's announcement means that by next March we shall be 750 guns ahead of a peacetime schedule which was drawn up four years before.
I am not blaming the John Inglis plant. If we take into consideration the fact that they started from nothing, they have probably gone into production as quickly as possible. But I would suggest that the fact that by next March we are going to be able to equip fewer than thirty^five infantry battalions, fewer than 35,000 men, when we have 150,000 men in training in Canada-and that is on the
498	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Douglas (Weybum)
basis of only one light machine gun to a section-indicates a Sony example of muddling and inefficiency. The house has a right to know whether the government contemplates putting other firms or some of the other government arsenals into the production of the Bren machine gun.
The committee which I suggested should be set up ought to be given information about the production of 25-pounders. So far, I understand, we are not producing any. Above all, we have a right to know something about the real facts as to aircraft production in Canada. Some of the glowing statements issued to the press about the number of aeroplanes being produced each month omit to tell the public that, of course, these are planes without engines. There is a growing feeling among men who are acquainted with the aircraft industry that something is seriously wrong. I am told by experienced pilots that the Boeing aeroplane is one of the four best aircraft in the world. If that is true, why is the Boeing aeroplane factory in Vancouver being allowed practically to close its doors? I came down in the train with aircraft mechanics let out of the Boeing plant because the plant officials said they could not get sufficient raw materials and, therefore, must curtail production. Surely there is something wrong there. Further, may I refer the house to the Malton plant near Toronto owned by the National Steel Car Corporation. This is said to be one of the best equipped plants in the country. The Canadian government's original educational contract was for twenty-eight Lysander planes. This plane, it is said, is regarded by authorities today as being the best army cooperation plane produced, and the need for mass production of these planes is most urgent. As I understand it, the educational contract called for the first planes to be completed and delivered by November, 1939, but up to December, 1939, only twenty-four of the twenty-eight had been completed for delivery, and the last four were not finished until March, 1940. Since January, 1940, three contracts for Lysander planes have been begun, but prior to October 5 not one Lysander plane under the new contracts had been completed for delivery from the Malton shop.
Hon. members have a right to know what is wrong. Men who have worked in that plant are enthusiastic about its equipment, but in the last few months at least a dozen key men have quit their jobs, among these men being the plant manager, the chief plant superintendent, the chief plant inspector, the erection and shop foreman, the machine-shop foreman and the plant's test pilot. The estimate given to me is that the employee turn-over at Malton during the past year

has been from 75 to 90 per cent, and that more than 900 men have quit their jobs in the plant during the past six months.
I have a great deal more information about that plant, but I refer to it now merely to point out that there ought to be some representative body of this house to whom such information could be given and before whom such matters could be discussed. Let me tell the government now that the people of Canada are in no mood to stand for bungling and inefficiency, and that we in this house have a responsibility to see to it that the men who are going to risk their lives in defence of democracy are getting the very best equipment that human ingenuity and skill can produce.

speechtext:
Last year I
suggested to the house and to the government that the public accounts committee or some similar body representative of all parties in the house ought to be allowed to examine war contracts. This has not been done. It is true that the Department of Munitions and Supply have issued long lists of contracts, but they have neither meaning nor value, because they are not classified and do not give the amounts obtained or the unit prices. It is of little value to any member to know that the government has spent half a million dollars in buying boots unless we know what the boots cost per pair and the basis upon which the contract was let. After the experience of the last war, it is only natural that the Canadian people should be suspicious on the question of war profiteering; and the government, for its own sake and for the sake of the morale of the public, ought to bend over backwards in handling this matter.
Something has already been said with reference to sessional paper No. 121 tabled in this house on November 20. There are two significant facts about it. One is that, so it is said, it is not considered in the public interest to give unit prices on an order of 26,000 garbage cans ordered by the Department of Munitions and Supply earlier in the year. That is quite a number of garbage cans and they ought to hold a great deal of garbage. Since then, we have been given the unit prices, but I would call attention to the explanation of the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe). He says that the reason why they are reluctant to give unit prices is that competitors will see what the figures are. Well, do we not want competitive bidding? Do we not want to buy articles at the lowest prices at which they can be purchased on

The Address-Mr. Douglas (Weybum)
the market? Why should the house not be given unit prices on any of these commodities, except with regard to those of secret design? The second and more significant fact is that, of the 26,000 cans ordered, 20,950 were ordered from General Steel Wares Limited-four-fifths of the order-and the assistant general manager of Steel Wares Limited is or was Mr. G. K. Sheils, deputy minister of the Department of Munitions and Supply.
I suggest that this sort of thing does not make for confidence and enthusiasm on the part of the Canadian public, who have been bled so often in days gone by. Therefore, at the risk of wearying the government, I will repeat the request I made last year: first, that the government consider setting up a committee to receive information with regard to the success that we are having in producing war material; and, second, that the public accounts committee or some other committee be allowed to examine war contracts.
I know the government does not like criticisms of this sort and is inclined to view them as a personal reflection. No such reflection is intended. I would remind the house that a year ago in the French chamber of deputies similar criticisms were met with indignant denials and soothing assurances that all was well. We know now that all was not well. A similar set of conditions obtained in Great Britain, where for years Mr. Winston Churchill was a voice crying in the wilderness against mismanagement and incompetence; but his criticisms were labelled unpatriotic and subversive, and were taken by some cabinet ministers as a reflection upon their personal integrity rather than as an indication of their unfitness for the positions they held. That attitude should not prevail here.
If all is well in our war effort, then the government should not hesitate for a moment to make the facts available, if not to the house at least to a committee of the house. And if all is not well, then we had better find it out now rather than wait until our house lies in ruins about us. In France and the United Kingdom it took a series of reverses to bring the people to their senses. Surely in this country we can learn by the experience of others and not wait until catastrophe jolts us out of our complacency. If there is a bottleneck somewhere; if lack of certain essential equipment is due to the organization of the Department of Munitions and Supply, then that department ought to be overhauled and overhauled immediately, because the Canadian people will hold this government and every member of this house responsible if they discover that incompetence,
bungling or partisanship has caused us to do less than we ought to be doing in the prosecution of the war.
In dealing with Canada's war effort I wish to add my voice to those of others who have asked the government to give free transportation to members of the Canadian active service force. I hope the statement of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) will not be taken as final. Coming down on the train, I met a'ycnmg man from Nanaimo, British Columbia, who for over a year has been a member of a forestry corps which is now stationed at Valcartier, Quebec. He has been away from home for a year. He finally got his furlough, but found that, to go home, it would cost him about S100 for travelling and incidentals. Only the fact that some friends sent him the money made it possible for him to go home and see his wife and family.
The unit in which I am especially interested is the first battalion of the South Saskatchewan regiment which is now stationed in Toronto. I have over a score of letters from men in that unit and units similarly situated telling me there is being circulated among the men a list asking whether they want to go home for Christmas or New Year's, and the answer is invariably the same:
" It does not make any difference because we cannot afford to go home anyway." It would cost these men at least $35 to $50 for transportation, and on a soldier's pay, particularly if he is married, he cannot possibly raise that money.
I would remind the house that some of these men will be going overseas shortly, and the forty-eight hours' fembarkation leave is not enough to allow them to go home; thus for many of them this Christmas or New Year's leave will be the last opportunity they will have of being reunited with their families prior to crossing the ocean and facing all the dangers of war. Surely the government which is finding money for so many other things can see to it that these men are able to go home and spend what for some of them may be their last Christmas with their loved ones round the family hearth.
I wish now to deal with a problem which is the very opposite of that of the fighting forces. I refer to individuals across this country who are known as conscientious objectors. I have never been a pacifist. As hon. members know, ever since coming to this house in 1936 I have advocated economic, and, if needs be, military sanctions against aggressor nations.	I have never been a
pacifist because I believe that, in the Christian concept of society, "those who are strong ought to bear the burdens of the weak", and
500	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Douglas (Weybum)
that those who have the strength and the will are responsible for defending the helpless and the weak from injustice and oppression. For that reason I have never been able to accept the pacifist philosophy.
But while I do not agree with the pacifists I am prepared to fight to the death for a man's right to be a pacifist. The right of conscience is as old as Christianity, which has taught through the centuries that we must render unto Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and unto God the things that are God's. Christianity has taught that the individual has a right to determine where his duty to Caesar ends and his duty to God begins. Some of us in this house are descendants of the Scottish covenanters, of whom it was said:
They counted their faith so grand a thing They scorned to yield it to a king.
The reason why we are opposing Hitler to-day is that he has denied that right of conscience, and has said that the will of the state is supreme over the will of the individual. We do not believe that. But we cannot defeat Hitler by emulating Hitler.
In the regulations set out under the National War Services Act there is a provision for conscientious objectors. It is regulation 18, which reads:
Conscientious Objectors 18. (1) Any man who, from the doctrines of his religion, is averse to bearing arms or undertaking combatant service, may apply for an order deferring or postponing his military training indefinitely, provided that it is established that such man conscientiously objects to the bearing of arms or the undertaking of combatant service and-
I draw the attention of hon. members to that word "and", which I think ought to be "or".
-is prohibited from the bearing of arms or undertaking combatant service by the tenets and articles of faith in effect on the first day of September, 1939, of any organized religious denomination to which said man aforesaid, in good faith, belongs.

I draw this to the attention of the house because in the city of Saskatoon a group of young men appeared before a government tribunal and were refused the right of exemption, not because they could not establish that they

had conscientious objections to bearing arms, but because some of them did not belong to a church which prohibits the bearing of arms. Most of them belonged to the United church, I think one to the Anglican church.
I am asking the Minister of National War Services (Mr. Gardiner) to consider in this matter three things: first, that regulation 18 should be amended to give the individual the right of exemption because of his conscientious scruples, irrespective of the stand of any church to which he might or might not belong; second, that the minister should consider the advisability of giving to divinity students studying for the Protestant ministry the same right of exemption that may be given to those in any other religious order; and, third, that a list of alternative non-combatant services be set out and that training be given along these lines for those who have conscientious objection to the bearing of arms, because I do not believe that in this hour of crisis any man has a right to exemption from service, but I do believe that he has a right to determine what service he can conscientiously perform.
I turn now to the defence of Canada regulations, as having an important part in our war effort. I recognize, as must every hon. member, the need for taking strict measures against espionage and sabotage if we are to prevent our country from being undermined. At the same time I must insist, as have other hon. .members, that these regulations shall not be used to repress freedom of speech or of the press or to interfere with workers or farmers who are seeking to organize with a view to bettering their economic standard of living. I am in accordance with the suggestions of the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) and the views of the hon. member for North Battleford (Mrs. Nielsen).

speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman allow me to ask a question? Has he given any consideration to the question of the entire suspension of the writ of habeas corpus, so far as internees are concerned, under the defence of Canada regulations? That is very important.

speechtext:
As the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) will perhaps remember, in the discussion last year of the defence of Canada regulations, when the committee was being set up to study them, we objected to that right being taken from internees. We contend that it is so easy in times like these when we are all naturally susceptible to some hysteria, to let our fears of fifth columnists become a screen behind

The Address-Mr. Douglas (Weybum)
which we allow reactionary forces to destroy some of the very things for which we profess to be fighting.
I have a concrete example that I wish to place before -the house. I have a brief here from the legal counsel who was concerned with this case and who, I know, would be glad to place this material personally before a committee of the house.
A short time ago relief recipients working for the city of Regina went on strike. Consequently, the relief committee of the city council and some members of the council invited a delegation of three from the relief recipients to interview them at the city hall. At that meeting there were none present except the delegation of three, the relief committee of the Regina city council and the officials of the provincial government interested in relief matters. Therefore there was really no one there except those definitely interested in the submissions to be made by the delegation from the relief recipients.
The three men submitted their case, the first two members of the delegation putting forth their claims for wages and work, and the third member, Mr. Florian Stephan, drawing particularly to the attention of the committee how the relief recipients felt about the relief situation. As soon as that meeting was over, two members of the Regina city council went to the police station and laid a charge against Stephan under the defence of Canada regulations, more particularly under that section which deals with the making of inflammatory statements with a view to causing disaffection towards his majesty. No summons was issued, but this man was arrested and thrown into gaol.
The only evidence put forth by the crown at the trial was that of a very third-rate stenographer who took notes of the speech. She admitted that she did not get down correctly the statements made, and that she had not had a great deal of experience as a stenographer. Mr. Hark MacPherson, chairman of the relief committee, admitted on the stand that there had been the friendliest atmosphere possible at the meeting and that he saw nothing in the speech that would alarm or disturb him. Other witnesses gave evidence to the same effect. The members of the relief recipients' delegation swore on the stand that the speech given by Stephan was quite different from the copy under which he was charged. I have a copy here of what he is alleged to have said; and in spite of the fact that the witnesses declared that it did not represent a fair report of his statement, personally I can see nothing wrong with it.

Not to my

The only thing I wish to state, and I want you people to take this seriously. These people who walk off these jobs did not do it for fun, and do not underestimate these people. It is a serious matter to them. They have suffered to an extent where continuance was unbearable.
I know, and everybody knows, that since this war we have been pinched, and millions made by certain people in the war. Therefore, there is an attitude among those people. These people have nothing but suffering, and they are prepared to suffer much more in order to get the elementary basis of living, and they are not getting it, and I can say that they are willing to suffer much more in order to gain. They will insist upon this. They were free once. In plain words, they are fed up by being demanded by rules and regulations, for when a man is earning his money, for God's sake give him that money and let him be free. That is the general opinion of the people, and they believe they earn everything and get nothing for it. There is a lot of sentiment and sympathy, in the way of donations of a department store already received. There are a number of grocers and stores who have shown favour, and feel that we have a just ease. And the people who have suffered are willing to suffer more and knowing of the support of the average man and citizen in this city, they are prepared to continue and carry on. I do not wish this as a threat, but just realize the gravity of the situation and how they feel. They know you can use a strong arm, but I know they are absolutely sincere and I know that is their stand with no idea of threat and I sincerely hope some agreement can be made.

That is the complete statement, as I have it from the counsel. For making that statement, a nominal fine of $10 and costs was imposed on Florian Stephan; a conviction has been registered against him, and he has been photographed and finger-printed like a common convict. Apparently his only crime was that he made an appeal to the relief committee of the Regina city council to prevent schisms and divisions among our people, pointing out that there was need of a better feeling between employer and labour, and that those who exploited the common people were doing far greater disservice to the state than the fifth columnists themselves. Surely it is indicative of the road along which we are travelling when a man whose only crime is seeking to get better conditions for himself and his

The Address-Mr, Douglas (Weyburn)
fellow workers can be hauled into court, merely by some local body under the authority of the provincial attorney general, without any representation having been made to the Minister of Justice or the federal government. I would not like that in Germany, Mr. Speaker; I like it a great deal less when it happens in my own province. On behalf of our group I wish to say that we will continue to demand that these regulations be amended. We do not want to make it easier for the fifth columnists. If we had our way we would make it a great deal harder for the fifth columnists, but we desire to make sure that innocent people cannot be prevented by these regulations from exercising those prerogatives which, under democracy, belong to every citizen of the state.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, when the house rose at six o'clock I was asking the house to give consideration to a programme for western agriculture. Before continuing with my remarks, I should like to refer to a rather sneering reference which was made by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) to members of this group. He said that only one of us had ever earned his living on the farm. Surely the Minister of Agriculture is not going to pose here as a farmer who has turned politician. Those of us who come from Saskatchewan know perfectly well that he is really a politician turned farmer. As a matter of fact, the Minister of Agriculture began his public career as a school-teacher. It was only when he had entered the Saskatchewan legislature that he took up^ farming, which he has used ever since as a shield for his other activities.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Was he not a farmer before he was a politician?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Not to my knowledge, except that as a boy he probably lived on the farm. I should like, however, to tell the minister that there is no disgrace in not having lived on the farm. In my opinion, the only disgrace is to have been elected by farmers and then, after coming to Ottawa, to have turned round and sold them out, as they have been sold out for the last twenty-five years.
The minister said that his agricultural policies were endorsed by the farmers in the last federal election. If there is any man in the government who ought not to mention the last federal election, it is the Minister of Agriculture. He represents Saskatchewan in the cabinet, and Saskatchewan was the only province where the government came out of the election with fewer seats than they had before. They went into the election with seventeen seats and came out with twelve. No small part of that reduction was due to the same minister and his policies. An examination of the results from the rural polls will show that the minister was ignominously defeated by the farmers of his own constituency. He was rescued by the vote of the town people and by the fact that a third candidate was kept in the field to split the vote. The minister says that he was elected by agriculture, but the fact is that he was elected in spite of agriculture. In my opinion, agriculture in this country is important enough to deserve the full time and exclusive attention of one minister of the crown. I do not think the Canadian farmer will take well to the fact that he is represented by a minister who is half-time Minister of Agriculture and half-time Minister of National War Services. From now on we shall have to call him "minister of half and half".
The problem of agriculture divides itself into two parts:	First, there is the problem having to do with those who have no crops, and, second, there is the problem having to do with those who have crops.
Like most western members I was delighted when the Minister of Agriculture announced that 1940 would be declared an emergency year under section 3 of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. That is excellent, and I hope the government will accede to the application of the province of Saskatchewan to have a crop failure area declared under section 4 of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. There are in Saskatchewan somewhere between 170 and 200 townships which ought to qualify under that section of the act. If they do not qualify,

The Address-Mr. Douglas (Weyburn)
then the people living therein will have to come under section 3, which means that they will receive 50 cents an acre less by way of bonus. But what is more important, they will receive no benefit from the $200 minimum which applies only if a crop failure area is declared.
I would remind the government that there are people who will not get the bonus, and there are others who will need some assistance until they do get the bonus, especially if it is as late as it was last year. In many districts the people cannot get relief because the municipalities in which they live cannot afford to pay their 20 per cent share. I still think there is need for an emergency relief fund to provide for people who cannot be taken care of by their local municipalities.
I should like to say a word about those people who have a crop. The acting leader of this group, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), has already outlined an agricultural programme and I intend merely to touch upon it. The first suggestion was that the government should make an interim payment on the 1939 wheat crop. Farmers of western Canada were led to believe that they would get this if the present government were elected. Second, I urge that consideration be given to paying an advance for wheat stored on the farms. I would remind the government that in the latter part of July and early in August of last year the groups in this corner and the official opposition advocated such an advance being made. Replying to us, the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar) is reported as follows at page 2420 of Hansard:
I say to them once more that the government are not unsympathetic to the suggestions they have advanced.
As reported on page 2421, I put the following question to and received the following answer from the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon):
If the minister will get up and say that the farmer will get a cash advance on the grain which he is not able to sell to the wheat board I am prepared to stop debating the matter.
Mr. MacKinnon (Edmonton West):	All I
can say is that the wheat committee of the cabinet is seeking a solution right along the line indicated by the hon. member for Weyburn.
We left here with the impression that something of that sort would be done. Nothing of that sort has been done, and no reason has been given why it could not be done. We heard the other day from the Minister of Trade and Commerce that the farmers had a reserve of some $100,000,000, but this wheat is not a reserve. This wheat represents frozen assets; it represents money
which the farmer cannot get; it represents goods which he cannot sell. But in the meantime his debts are going unpaid.
Third, we advocated the closing of the Winnipeg grain exchange during the war. Fourth, we advocated the handling of all wheat through the wheat board and, fifth, the bringing down of an agricultural policy for the handling of the 1941 wheat crop. I am in agreement with the suggestion made by other hon. members in this and othei opposition groups that it might be wise tc have a higher initial payment on a limitec quantity of wheat, and then lower the price to a fixed minimum, as the amount of wheal increased. In other words, allow the farmei to deliver his wheat at a graduated price This would encourage the farmer to produce a certain quantity of wheat, but would not encourage him to overproduce.
I hope the government will give some consideration to this problem, because to ask the farmer to continue to produce wheat at a price which is admitted by the government itself as being inadequate is to ask western Canada to assume almost certain economic bankruptcy in the next few years.
I should like to close my remarks with just one more observation. If this war has done nothing else, it has given a new sense of dignity to the common man. Speaking over the radio the other day, J. B. Priestley said:
It is not the British ruling class, which wobbled and whined for years until Herr Hitler was firmly established, that has aroused the admiration of the world, but the common people of Britain, who have come out of their sleep not only to defend such liberties as they already have but also to demand more liberty.
I think that is true. I think we have come more and more to appreciate the common man, the sailors who sail the sea and the people who work in our factories. We are beginning to realize the courage, the endurance and the high idealism of the man on the street. I think we all realize that this war cannot be won unless we have the support and enthusiasm of the common people.

speechtext:
I am very
much in sympathy with my hon. friend's recommendation for free transportation for the soldiers. I do not think the government could do anything which would go further toward raising the morale of the personnel of our fighting services than to carry out the recommendation of the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church). In the winning of this war morale is one of the all-important factors, and that morale can best be main-

7 he Address-Mr. Douglas (Weyburn)
tained by dealing with the very things I have mentioned-fair prices for the fanner, better working conditions for the common people, the rights of labour to organization and collective bargaining.
These are difficult days through which we are passing. I remember two years ago listening to a professor friend of mine in the city of Chicago who had spent some time with Doctor Charles Beard, the great American historian who wrote the "Rise of American Civilization." One night my friend said that he and another professor walked home with Doctor Beard and one of them asked him, "How long would it take you, Doctor Beard, to write and tell the world what you have learned from a lifelong study of history?" "I could do it," said Doctor Beard after thinking for a minute, "in three years." He walked along for a while and then said, "I could do it in three months." A few moments later he said, "I could do it in three days," and finally he said, "I could do it in four sentences." He wrote those four sentences down, and I pass them on to this house.
The first one was: "Whom the gods would destroy they first make mad." I ask the house to think to-night of some megalomaniacs who have plunged the world into war and bloodshed and tears.
His second sentence was: "The mills of the gods grind slowly, yet they grind exceeding small." I ask this house to think how the forces of righteousness and justice have triumphed down through the ages in spite of opposition and betrayal.
His third sentence was: "The bee fertilizes the flower that it robs." I ask this house to think of China to-night and of all the other countries that are being despoiled and robbed and which, even yet, out of their hour of tragedy, may find the dawn of a better day.
His fourth sentence was this: "Sometimes, if it is dark enough, you can see the stars."
I submit that out of the darkness through which this country, in common with other parts of the world, is passing, we may see the stars, and two of those stars are the dignity of man and the worth of human brotherhood.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has spoken of the earnestness of the Liberal government's war effort, and other ministers of the crown have told us of the rather slow growth of our armed forces, but no minister of the crown has told us whether the government has a policy of coordination of our war effort based on a strategic plan. I think the members of this house should be informed whether or not the government has a policy of coordination 
among the war departments responsible for the development of our army, navy and air force based on a strategic plan. If the government had no such policy, I would suggest that it give the matter its very earnest consideration.
We are now, I believe, in a position to take a clearer view of our military situation than we were when the house adjourned on August 7 last. The battle of Britain, or rather the first phase of that battle, has been fought and the attempt at invasion has for the time being been defeated. It must now be apparent to all of us that if this war is to be brought to a successful conclusion, it is of the utmost importance that we obtain superiority in the air. That is essential. Up to the present time I believe we have not obtained parity in the air, despite the wonderful achievements of our heroic air force.
The Right Hon. Winston Churchill, speaking in the British house on the 5th of this month, said that Great Britain was on the road to parity in the air. It will be noted that he did not say that we have achieved parity in the air. Then he added that superiority in the air was indispensable before we could gain victory. That being the situation, it seems to me that the government at the present time should direct its major effort to the development of our air force. The development of our air force should be given priority, and if any conflict of interest arises between the demands of our army, our navy and our air force, the government should insist that the requirements of .the air force be given first consideration, that the department presided over by the Minister of National Defence for Air (Mr. Powder) be given the right of way. I came across an extract from an article published recently in the Winnipeg Free Press which has some bearing on this matter, and I propose to read it to the house. I quote:
Is Canada doing the right thing in spending almost two dollars on her army for every dollar spent on the air force? The big army school of thought seems to dominate our military thinking. Is it wise that this should be so? Has the government thoroughly thought out all the implications of our present war plan m relation to the broad needs for victory? Under what circumstances do they envisage the need to have a bigger army than air force? Is it for the defence of our own shores? Or is it to contribute the needed infantry and mechanized divisions for the land attack on the continent of Europe envisaged by General Crerar, our chief of staff, in a recent address?
When all is said and done, our material resources and our man-power are not unlimited, and ever-increasing demands are being made upon them. If these demands should result in any conflict of interest between the differ-

The Address-Mr. Eaten
ent branches of our fighting forces, in my opinion the demands of the air force should have first consideration.
I am not unmindful of the importance of the services that have been and will be rendered by our army and navy, but I submit that at the present time our greatest effort should be directed to the development of our air force and that this effort should not be hindered by any demand by our army or by our navy.
I should like to draw the attention of the government to the waste that has been going on in the construction of military camps in New Brunswick. I believe some waste is going on in some of the other provinces. This matter was brought to the attention of the government by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) when he spoke in this debate, and I thought that the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston), when he replied, treated that matter with less seriousness than it deserved. The day after I returned to Saint John on the adjournment of this house in August last, I was approached by a man whom I knew but slightly, the manager of a local insurance company, who told me that he had just got back from the camp at Sussex and that he was shocked at the waste that was going on there. His chief complaint was that the lumber which was going into those camps was planed on the four sides.
A day or two later I had a visit from a prominent farmer, a thoroughly practical man from Elgin, in Albert county. He told me that he had been to the camp and that the waste which was going on there was terrible. He said that the specifications required the lumber which went into the huts to be planed on four sides, and that this meant that after the lumber was manufactured in some mills it had to be loaded on trucks, carted away to other mills where it was planed, reloaded on trucks and brought back to the camp at Sussex. He told me also that the water system and the sewerage system for those huts were laid down in two different trenches, when, he said, one trench would have been sufficient.
I visited the camp at Sussex. The Minister of National Defence has told us that the camp, which consists, I believe, of 148 huts, is costing $1,800,000. While I am not a builder or a contractor, I could see no reason why the lumber which was going into the camps had to be planed on four sides, and I believe that thousands of dollars have been needlessly expended because of that requirement. The matter,. I submit, should be investigated.
The Minister of National Defence told us in the course of his speech that he had obtained a very competent engineer and that this engineer, with certain officers from the quartermaster-general's branch, was going to visit practically all the camps for the purpose of making a comparison between the cost of the camps which were put up by contract and the cost of the camps which were put up by the engineering service of the army. I suggest to the minister that he employ a competent architect and a competent accountant to make an investigation, without any officers from the quartermaster-general's branch, for the purpose of ascertaining what waste has resulted from the unnecessarily high specifications which were called for by the army in relation to those huts.
I realize that waste in war time is unavoidable, on account of the haste with which work has to be done. But there should be no waste as a result of stupidity, and it seems to me that when the army calls for too high specifications in connection with the construction of huts which will be needed for only a comparatively short time, there should be a check-up and the practice should be stopped as soon as possible.
One of the unfortunate consequences of this extravagance is that many people visited these camps when they were in course of construction and saw the waste which was going on, and their reaction was:	" The
government tells us to save our money and invest it in war securities, but why should we lend our money to the government to be wasted in this manner?" That is one regrettable result of wasteful expenditures by governments in war time.
I thought it possible that this waste was confined to one or more camps in New Brunswick. But the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling), who addressed this house the other day, spoke of the waste and political patronage which accompanied the erection of the camp at Vernon, British Columbia. We may be right in concluding that there has been waste in all the camps constructed throughout the dominion by the government for army purposes.
Another matter to which I should refer is political patronage. My information is that the practice still continues. I know that some members of the government-the war committee, I believe-issued last summer a statement to the effect that there was to be no more patronage in connection with war contracts. That was a very proper statement, and I believe that the ministers were sincere when they issued it, although I am not prepared to say that staunch party men,
The Address-Mr. Hazen

such as they, are not apt at times to be influenced both consciously and unconsciously by political motives. But make no mistake about it, in spite of that statement political patronage has not ceased to exist. Political patronage continues. The political machine is very difficult to control, and it has not been controlled. The unfortunate result is that people in this country still speak of the effort we are making as a "Liberal war." That is much to be regretted, but until we have some form of union or national government, that opinion will continue to exist.
I submit that it is a very strong argument for some form of union or national government, despite the fact that when it is brought about, the Prime Minister may run the risk of being " stabbed in the breast."
I had intended to speak this evening about free transportation for soldiers going on leave, but so many members have done so already, all of them being of opinion that soldiers going on leave should be given free transportation, that I will not elaborate on the matter. From what was said to-day, apparently the government cannot see its way clear to grant this concession, but I hope it will be able to reconsider its decision. If it cannot, I suggest that it give attention to reducing still further the price soldiers have to pay for their transportation; and if that cannot be done, at least let the government consider the desirability of arranging that, when soldiers go on leave, the paymasters of their units will give them advances, which can later be gradually repaid.
The only other point to which I wish to , refer in connection with soldiers' leave is that the matter was brought to the attention of the house and the government last May by two hon. members who sit on this side, and the then Minister of National Defence, Mr. Rogers, promised it his consideration. But evidently nothing was done, and the only decision which has been arrived at, the one reached lately, is that soldiers are not to be given free transportation when they go on leave. I think that is very much to be regretted.
I intended also to bring to the attention of this house the suggestion of a further reduction in rates on letters and parcels which are sent to our soldiers overseas. But that matter has also been brought to the attention of the government in the course of this debate, and I will not enlarge upon it.
I would urge that the government give the matter further consideration and that, if at all possible, a reduction be made in the postage on parcels that are sent to our soldiers overseas.

I would urge also that the government expedite the handling of mail both to and from these soldiers. I am under the impression, from my own experiences, that civilian mail to and from Great Britain is handled with greater expedition than the mail sent to our soldiers or the letters they send back to us. I understand that the government have this matter under investigation and I hope they will take such steps as will ensure that mail to and from the men overseas is delivered more promptly. It is a continuing source of uneasiness to parents, wives, children and, I fancy, to the soldiers themselves that mail is not delivered more promptly.
While I am on this subject I would suggest that the government see to it that the parcels which are sent to our soldiers overseas are given better protection and are delivered to the persons to whom they are addressed. Too many parcels disappear in the mail, not through any enemy action but from other causes. They do not reach the soldiers to whom they are addressed. Not long ago I received a letter from a private serving overseas in an infantry unit. In this letter, which is dated September 29, he says:
I have not received a parcel yet and I know some were sent on August 1. We have had parcels sent from home, cigarettes especially, and have been here two months and none of us have received any cigarettes yet.
This matter was evidently preying on his mind, for later on in his letter he refers to it again. He says:
I have not received a parcel yet and I know some were sent on August 1.
He continues:
Here is a good chance for you to go to town on better protection for mail and parcels.
I do not know whether I am "going to town", but I do urge the government and particularly the Postmaster General (Mr. Mulock) to see to it that better protection is given parcels sent overseas to our soldiers.
I have discussed one phase of this letter; may I refer to it from another point of view. The hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas) this afternoon called attention to a certain excess of zeal that had developed under the defence of Canada regulations. He told us about a committee of three, representing the unemployed in Regina, having conferred with the relief committee and with the Regina council. One of the people on relief made a speech outlining to the council and the relief committee the feelings of the men who were on relief, and the result was that a charge was laid against him under the defence of Canada regulations. He was brought before

The Address-Mr. Hazen
a magistrate and fined ten dollars. That is not what the defence of Canada regulations were intended for.
The other evening the hon. member for North Battleford (Mrs. Nielsen) told us how the provincial police of Saskatchewan had gone from house to house-I do not know what authority they could possibly have- collecting copies of a leaflet which had been distributed, and which contained a synopsis of a speech she had made on the budget in this house at the last session.
Freedom of speech and freedom of the press must be preserved in Canada. The defence of Canada regulations should not be taken advantage of and should not be carried out stupidly. Read any ordinary English newspaper like the Daily Mail and you will see from time to time the severe criticism that appears in it against the actions of the British government. Free speech is permitted in England, as this letter which I hold in my hand will show-I propose to read it into the record. It is written by a private serving in a Canadian infantry unit overseas. He is a married man, and before the war he made a living working longshore, driving a truck, doing whatever he could. Sometimes it was pretty hard to get a job, but he did the best he could to support his wife and family. He says:
Was to London for a week-end and was in Hyde park all p.m. and until twelve then had to walk to Union Jack club in an air raid and sleep on the floor of the club.
I believe we have talked of free speech in Hyde park and now I'd believe any story I heard of Hyde park. Can you imagine a country practically an armed camp yet a speaker with a red flag preaching communism unmolested, a Sinn Feiner from Ireland calling Churchill anything but a gentleman. A speaker freely admitting that he was a fifth columnist, and would be as long as capital crucified labour as at present. A speaker from the bureau of information, a woman on moral and sexual hygiene, and religious sects of all sorts . . . a Catholic priest. Then, the cream of the crop, an Abyssinian prince, educated at Oxford, he had about 3,000 people for an audience and kept them singing, laughing or crying, as he willed. He is often quoted in the press and referred to as "Prince Brotherly Love". He wears a colourful costume and turban, carries a union jack over one shoulder and a tricolour over the other, and he kept waving them at the other speakers and shouting "There's enough red in this flag for anyone". He told jokes that he made up himself. One of his remarks was "The best flag on earth, the sun never sets on it and wages never rise under it". Another was "Hitler says we are starving here, we're rationed on everything yet no one is hungry," then said he wras dry and in a minute be had about a bushel of sweets and even a bottle of pop, then he says "and Hitler says we're starving".
While this crowd were in one end of the park, bombs were dropping at the other end and no one moved away until midnight.
I have met a lot of people who have moved out of London, homes lost, business men who have been ruined yet all are cheerful and determined that Britain must win.
In the speech from the throne we were told that the government intended to introduce measures at this session of the house "for the prosecution of the war to the utmost of our strength." What these measures are, we do not know. Although three weeks have passed, the order paper remains a blank. Apparently the government have no legislation ready for us. They are proceeding in this matter with the same lack of energy that they displayed during the first eight or nine months of the war. The powers that have been conferred on the government by the War Measures Act and thq orders in council passed under its authority, together with the National Resources Mobilization Act passed at the last session of this house, have given the government almost dictatorial powers. The government have been given power to carry on this country's war effort "to the utmost of our strength", with one important qualification to which I shall refer in a moment. The government has been given power, to use the words of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cardin) in the eloquent and powerful speech he made in this house last June, the broadest blank cheque ever given to the executive of any parliament for the administration of public affairs and for the security of the nation.
What steps does the government propose to take under the great powers that it now possesses and has possessed for five or six months? How does it propose to organize our resources? To what extent does it propose to organize them? We have had only a limited and partial answer to these questions. We have not had a full answer. We do not know to-day how or to what extent the government proposes to mobilize the resources of this country under the great powers it now possesses.
We do know, however, that it is not the intention of the government to have conscription of man-power for the army or the navy or the air force for what we all realize to-day is Canada's first line of defence.

The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) said the other day that he stressed in July last that our first line of defence was the island fortress of Britain. But it is not the intention of the government to have conscription for our first
The Address-Mr. Hazen

line of defence; it proposes only to have conscription in our own peaceful country and its territorial waters.
In a Canadian Press dispatch from Montreal of August 14 last the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) is reported to have said in a broadcast over the Canadian Broadcasting system that he recalled a radio address he gave in June in which he declared himself against conscription of man-power for overseas service, and added, "I repeat this evening, overseas service remains voluntary." How the government, in the light of what has happened, can reconcile a policy of voluntary service overseas with the fact that our first line of defence is overseas and that if our first line of defence falls, we shall be in the greatest jeopardy, is something I have never been able to understand. It is lacking in logic; it is lacking in realism, foresight and energetic leadership.
We know that the government does not intend to mobilize the man-power of this country for service where it is most needed, in the actual theatre of war, but we do not know in any detail how it proposes to organize the resources of the country under the great powers that it possesses. Hon. members want to know and the country wants to know when, how and to what extent the government proposes to use the powers that have been given to it.
The hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Thorson) in the excellent speech he made here some days ago in this debate said:
Great Britain will need every possible assistance that we can give her and it is our solemn duty as a freedom loving nation to give her our maximum aid.
For this reason we, as members of parliament and representatives of the people, will wish to know, not only what progress has been made with our war effort-and we are proud of its increasing momentum-but, what is perhaps even more important at this stage of our war effort, we will wish to be informed as to what has not yet been done and what must still be done. Are there any deficiencies in our war effort? If so, what are they and what steps can be taken to remedy them? Are we running short of efficient man power in our war industries? If so, what efforts are being made to train men for special purposes? Is our war effort being restricted in any manner by financial considerations? If so, in what respect and how can these restrictions be removed?
These are all pertinent questions, to which we should be given candid and detailed answers by the government. Soothing words of reassurance that would leave us with a false sense of security are not satisfactory; they are not good enough.
Furthermore, we are not satisfied with the information, verging on political propaganda, that is handed out week by week by the

director of public information. We are told week after week that so many contracts totalling so many millions of dollars have been awarded by the Department of Munitions and Supply, and the contracts over $5,000 are listed. We are told also that so many construction contracts totalling so many more millions of dollars have been let. But we do not know in many instances, in fact in most instances, whether these contracts are being carried out, whether the orders are being filled, or what prices per unit are being paid for the goods bought. And we are never in these releases or anywhere else, as far as I know, told in any detail of any delays or difficulties that the government is experiencing in equipping our armed forces. By reading these releases that come to us from week to week we would be soothed into the happy frame of mind that the government has no difficulties and no problems. The policy adopted would appear to be that the idea must be created in the mind of the public that the political party that is carrying on this war is making a perfect job of it.

speechtext:
That is a dangerous policy and a policy that should be changed. The government have not made and are not, by any means, making a perfect job of our war effort.
The Minister of National Defence told us in the course of his speech that statistics regarding the rate of production and delivery of various items in connection with our war effort should not be made public, because to do so would furnish the enemy with information which he might spend millions of dollars to obtain. Then, in reply to some pertinent questions by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson), he said that no rifles will be manufactured until about the middle of July next, and that the production of 25-pounders will not be as early as expected but that a considerable number will be forthcoming in July, 1941. I am sure we all hope that these expectations will be realized, although the policy of better late than never is not a good one in war time. I am a little puzzled, however, as to why the minister should have furnished the house with this information, after telling us that the enemy should not be supplied with free information of this kind.
One subject upon which the Minister of National Defence did not touch during the course of his statement is the state of preparedness of our defences on the Atlantic and Pacific coasts. He did not tell us what steps, if any, had been taken to rebuild, modernize and improve those defences; nor did he tell us whether they are fully equipped

The Address-Mr. Hazen
with coastal artillery, anti-aircraft guns and searchlight batteries. Whether he omitted this information by accident or design, I do not know, but these are matters of importance. I trust that the development and equipment of these defences have been carried out, and that they are now in proper order.
The minister informed us also that he expected to visit the United Kingdom before long, in order to consult with the authorities there on matters of common interest. I am sure we all hold the Minister of National Defence in the highest regard; we wish him a safe voyage, and we hope and expect that his visit to England will result in furthering the war effort of this country.
In the course of his able address during this debate the leader of the opposition referred to a paragraph in the speech from the throne delivered by the deputy of the governor general when parliament was prorogued on November 5. The paragraph to which he drew attention stated that the measures taken by parliament during the session which was then being brought to a conclusion, had in view the immediate task of sharing more completely in the defence of Britain and securing our own country more effectively against internal subversion and external attack. The leader of the opposition said that these words were significant in that for the first time in Canada since we entered the struggle first things had been put first, that for the first time the government had recognized that the defence of Britain came first, and he congratulated the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) upon the words that had been used.
The Prime Minister, however, rather to my surprise, was critical of the remarks of the leader of the opposition. He said that he failed to see where the statement differed in any particular from the policy of the government as it was stated at the very outset of the war and as it had been followed since that time. He went on to quote from a broadcast he made on September 3, 1939, in which he said:
On Friday last the government, speaking on behalf of the Canadian people, anounced that in the event of the United Kingdom becoming engaged in war in an effort to resist aggression, they would as soon as parliament meets seek its authority for effective cooperation by Canada at the side of Britain.
That, he said, was the government's statement of policy before Britain herself had gone to war, and it was the policy the government had pursued ever since.
Well, Mr. Speaker, the words " effective cooperation" may be construed in a variety of ways. To many people who heard that address the words " effective cooperation "
may have meant defending our own shores and furnishing supplies to Britain, for which supplies we would be well paid; a merely perfunctory, safe and profitable cooperation. To others who listened to that address " effective cooperation '' may have meant not only what I have just stated but also a moderate and voluntary effort, without any conscription whatever.

The Prime Minister has
told us that his government has always followed the same policy, that it has always held the same position. If that is so; if there has been no change in his policy since September, 1939, all I can say is that many of the people who voted for him, aye, and some of the members who sit on his side of
The Address-Mr. Farquhar

the house to-day, failed to understand what he meant by that policy. For instance, last June, in this house the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. LaCroix) said:
. . . Mr. Speaker, I urge that we abide by the policy advocated by the Right Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King during the last elections, namely a voluntary and reasonable, measure of participation, without resorting in any way to conscription of man-power.
On the same occasion, speaking in the same debate, the hon. member for Laval-Two Mountains (Mr. Lacombe) said:
Mr. Speaker, I should be remiss in my duty if I failed to protest at once against the plan for mobilizing our man-power and wealth announced by the right hon. Prime Minister. This new policy is in glaring opposition to the electoral platform of the re-elected government. There was to be nothing but a moderate, voluntary and free war effort, we were told. I referred to that platform in this house on May 23 last. I was then speaking in defence of the Prime Minister, who was being harassed on all sides by the opposition.
The Prime Minister says that he has always pursued the same policy, but here is a member on his own side of the house who says that this is a new policy, and another who asks the Prime Minister to abide by the policy which he enunciated during the last election and says that this policy is in glaring opposition to the electoral platform of the re-elected government. All I can say is that these gentlemen all appear to be intelligent men, and it is unfortunate that there should be such a difference of opinion in connection with a policy which should be clear to all of us.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to say just a few words. This debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne is now drawing to a close, but before a vote is taken on the amendment moved by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) I should like to draw attention again to its wording. It says in part:
We respectfully submit to Your Excellency that this house regrets that the government has continued to soothe the Canadian people regarding the war effort of the nation, thereby creating a false sense of security when a clear-cut call to action is desperately needed.
When that amendment was moved by the leader of the opposition, I wondered what arguments would be brought forward by the members of the opposition in an effort to prove the truthfulness of the statements contained therein. I have listened to the debate in this house from day to day; I have read Hansard each day in order to make sure that I had overlooked nothing, and I ask any hon. member to show me where one argu-

ment has been brought forward which would prove in the slightest degree the truthfulness of the statement contained in the amendment moved by the leader of the opposition, that the government is continuing to soothe the people of Canada.
On the contrary, much has been said which would go to prove that the opposite is true. After listening to the statements made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the ministers of the various departments, I feel sure that there is not a member of the opposition but believes in his heart that the statements made in the amendment are far from the truth. I would go even further and say that the leader of the opposition himself does not believe that those statements are true, and I am quite sure that the people of Canada do not believe them. Had the leader of the opposition the information which he now has, I am quite sure that he would not have moved the amendment.
It is not unusual for the leader of the opposition to make statements in and out of the house which put him in wrong with his own followers and which lower the prestige of the party which he represents. I am hoping that he is not making another mistake at this time. Notwithstanding all the misstatements which the leader of the opposition has made, I still have a great deal of respect for him. I also hold many of his followers in very high regard because they are splendid fellows. In the light of all the information which we now have; in the light of all the facts which the ministers of the various departments have given us, I am going to ask the leader of the opposition to reconsider the statements which he has made and withdraw his amendment. If the leader of the opposition is the man which I give him credit for being, he will rise in his seat and withdraw his amendment.
