speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at a time when there is so much sorrow abroad in the world one is somewhat less inclined to be critical of those who are in places of great responsibility. Some of the members on the government _ side have expressed sympathy for the ministers, suggesting that they have been doing a great deal of work. No doubt they have been busy, and a good deal of credit is due them for that, but if there is anyone in this country who should be sympathized with, who should be given credit, it is the common people. They have endured much during the past years of depression and yet have come forward quite willingly to make every sacrifice they have been called upon to make, indeed, they have made sacrifices which I

The Address-Mr. Kuhl
consider are absolutely unessential. Yet they have come forward to offer their services in a hundred and one different ways.
The ministers at least have security, even though they may have to work hard. Should they suffer ill health, they are able to secure the best medical attention, but that cannot be said of the people of Canada at large. As I said, in times like this one is inclined to be rather less critical, but when one sees an enemy within the gates getting away with murder at a time when the common people are in a life and death struggle with an external enemy, one would have to be made of stone not to cry out against the monstrous injustice which is being done.
The enemy within our gates to which I refer is the money power. I know there are those who scoff at the suggestion of the existence of a money power, but was it not the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) himself who suggested in the campaign of 1935 that there was a money power? Was it not he who said that if he were elected to power he would do battle with the money power? If there is no money power, then the Prime Minister was deceiving the people. If there is a money power, then what happened in the battle? It is quite obvious that the battle never took place. The Liberal party pulled up the white flag before ever there was a battle.
I am inclined to believe that there is a money power. Every great leader who has attempted to do anything for his people has come into conflict with this monster of iniquity, the money power. We all know the conflict which Abraham Lincoln had with this money power, and how he paid with his own life. During the debate last year, I quoted some statements of Abraham Lincoln, where he said that he was fighting two enemies, and I should like to refer to them again. I believe that is the position in which the common people of Canada find themselves. They have not only an external enemy but an internal one as well. Abraham Lincoln in the American civil war is reported to have said:
I have two great enemies, the southern army in front of me and the financial institutions in the rear. Of the two the one in the rear is my greatest foe.
I am sure no one will suggest that Abraham Lincoln did not know what he was talking about. There is a money power at work in this country of ours, gnawing at the very vitals of this nation. There is in Canada an internal dictatorship just as diabolically wicked as the one with which we in the empire are in armed conflict. The people of Alberta have sent the Social Credit members to this parliament because they have come to the conclusion, not only as a result of studies
they have made but from actual experience, that there is a money power, and they have sent us here to do all in our power to fight this money power.
I wish also to say that the people who have sent the Social Credit members here are just as loyal citizens of Canada as any other people who send Liberal or Conservative members or members of any other party to this house. In fact I am quite persuaded that if the Canadian people were permitted to know the truth about money, banks and banking, a much larger number of social crediters, or at least of those who support monetary reform, would be sent to this house. But the sad fact of the situation is that the common people are prevented from getting the truth about money and about banks and banking. Millions are used by the bankers to defeat monetary reformers, to confuse the thinking of the people and deceive them into believing that which is not true.
We Social Credit members here intend to fight this money power as long as there is breath in our bodies. We are criticized quite frequently as being cranks on the subject of money and for talking about nothing but money. I suggest to the house that there is no more important subject that parliament could discuss than money. Every solitary thing that is discussed in this house hinges on money. Listen to any and every member talk and you will conclude that there is only one thing lacking, and that is a proper monetary policy. Every member, whether he is discussing war or peace problems of this country, admits or implies that the physical requirements are here to solve almost any problem. There are, of course, limitations in endeavouring to supply war equipment, but generally speaking every member admits or implies by what he says that physically there is nothing lacking, thereby implying that the only thing that is lacking is a proper financial policy. Consequently I do not think we are out of order in harping on the subject of money in season and out as long as we are here. In that connection I should like to quote a passage from Arthur Kitson in which he points out the enormous importance of the subject of money. He says:
The money question is the greatest moral and social question which mankind has ever had to consider. It concerns the lives, fortunes and happiness of every human being in society and of generations yet unborn. All other questions sink into insignificance compared with this one.
I agree with that statement one hundred per cent.
The hon. member for St. Antoine-West-mount (Mr. Abbott) in speaking the other
The Address-Mr. Kuhl

day-and no doubt he was making his remarks particularly for the benefit of members of the Social Credit group-said: "War machines are not created by money." That was just another sample of the straw men set up by those who try to refute the Social Credit argument. Then they knock down the straw man under the pretence that they are destroying the Social Credit argument. The hon. member cannot point to a single instance of a member of this group ever suggesting that money created things. No one ever said that money could create war machines. I do not say it, and none of our group ever said it. But what we do contend is that without money, war machines cannot be built. There is nothing that can be manufactured except through the use of money. In the days of barter when goods were traded for goods it was possible, but in the complex modern age in which we live money is absolutely essential, and without money, even though you have the men and the materials, you cannot bring them together to produce the things that are required. I do not think that can be controverted.
The money system, whatever we use for money to-day, is the heart, the blood, the most vital organ in our national economy. Without it our national life would be paralyzed. It is absolutely impossible to produce things in this modern world without having at one's command an adequate system of money.
I should like to ask those who suggest that money is not our trouble, why have we idle resources and idle men even to-day if there is a need for materials and for skilled men? Many members of the house have indicated in their addresses that there are many skilled workmen and skilled graduates of our youth training schools who are now out of employment. I am sure that every member has correspondence almost every day from people who desire work of one kind or another. If there are idle labour and idle materials; if we still have resources which are not being worked, why are they not being worked if the trouble is not a lack of money? Why is not the idle labour put to work on the idle resources? If factories are running to capacity, why are not men put to work enlarging the factories and plant equipment? If there should ever be a time when we run short of labour, skilled or unskilled, is it not a simple matter to obtain many men from the unemployed ranks in the United States? There are as many people in the ranks of the unemployed over there as there are people in the whole of Canada.
I wish again to emphasize that the one thing lacking in our national economy is an 
adequate money system. Day after day we have been listening to hon. members pleading with the government to grant soldiers free transportation on their Christmas leave. Why do the government say that they cannot do this? Is it because there is not accommodation in the railway cars? Is it because we have not enough engines or adequate railway equipment? Everyone knows that is not the situation. Trains are running up and down this country half-empty, and if there are not enough cars, why cannot more be manufactured? It is purely and simply a question of finance. What prevents our soldiers from getting free transportation home for Christmas is a financial, not a physical problem. I think it is a shame that young men who are placing their lives in jeopardy for this country should be treated in such a fashion. It is a question of money.
Consider any question which is raised in this house. Take, for instance the provision of storage for wheat. Surely one must concede upon the slightest reflection that that is purely a financial question. Are we without storage facilities because we lack lumber, or labour to produce the lumber, or cement to build storage? We are not lacking in anything physical. Then, why have we all these unemployed, these unused resources, this overripe timber? Every problem connected with this matter of the handling of grain is financial and nothing else.
Or take any other of the numerous agricultural problems which have been discussed in this chamber. I hear our Conservative friends from Ontario constantly bemoaning the fact that vegetables and fruit are admitted from across the border in competition with produce which is raised in their province. Again, is it not a question of finance? There are in this country hundreds of thousands of people who would like to supplement their diet with more vegetables, fruit, fish and poultry. We are doing a great deal of high-pressure advertising. The government tries by these advertisements to induce people to eat more apples, more lobsters, more fish. The government does not have to tell people what to eat. All that is wrong is that they have not the money to pay for these commodities. If the government sees to it that the financial system enables the people to make their demand effective, it will not need to carry on all this high-pressure advertising; it is just a waste of time, energy, and material.
The problem of the maritime provinces resolves itself into one of finance. People in the interior of Canada would like to have the products of the fishermen. They are not using them, not because they do not desire

The Address-Mr. Kuhl
to eat fish or because they do not know about it, but because their purchasing power does not permit them to buy these products.
The people of the prairie provinces would like to have the fruits of British Columbia, and British Columbia wants the grain of the prairie provinces. Why do they not exchange the one for the other? Not on account of physical handicaps; for railway trains are operating every day, many times with empty cars, going from one province to another. There are no physical limitations; the question resolves itself into one of finance and nothing else.
Or consider the question of allowances to the widows and dependents of war veterans. Why should these people not have complete economic security? Have we not sufficient of the amenities of life; have we not the physical resources to take care of these people? No one will deny that we have.
Again, the matter of taking care of those who are not able to take care of themselves resolves itself into a question of finance. The same is true of old age pensions. Certainly we have enough food, clothing and material to maintain and house our aged people. The physical requirements are here; we have every essential to .make them comfortable and happy during the sunset days of their lives. It is a question of an adequate financial policy- nothing else.
Consider the health standards of our people. One of the best contributions Canada can make to the war effort of the empire is to put its people in the best physical and mental health that is humanly possible. It is not being done. Why? Because the medical facilities are not there? No. There are plenty of doctors who have not sufficient practice; there are ample hospital facilities and all kinds of services to promote the health of the people; there are plenty of foodstuffs to provide them with diets which will build healthy bodies. The question of the health of the people of Canada is a question of finance-nothing else.
One could go on and enumerate every problem which has been raised by any hon. member in this house; when boiled down to its final essence, each one is a matter of finance and nothing else.
I suggest that the financial problem should not be difficult of solution. If our financial system to-day were dependent upon the minting and circulation of gold as a medium of exchange, we might be confronted with an impossible physical problem. Probably there would not be enough gold. But our money system to-day is simplicity itself. It is nothing more or less than a simple bookkeeping system. Ninety-five per cent of our money is nothing but drops of ink on pieces of paperthe simplest commodities in the world to obtain. This is the most easily operated, most easily controlled and most perfect money system that the mind of man has ever devised. It is almost costless to operate. It is purely bookkeeping. The great and palatial structures which are erected all over this dominion as bank buildings are quite unessential. The amount of materials consumed in administering the financial policy of this country is almost negligible.
Since the financial system in itself is so simple, why should it be so difficult to solve our financial problems? The evils of our financial system lie not in the system itself, but in the method under which it is operated, in the policy which is pursued. Although it is an almost perfect system, the most perfect which has ever been devised, it is one of the most ill-managed and ill-conducted; so much so that, though this Canada of ours, with its sparse population and enormous resources, makes us, physically speaking, millionaires, we have been brought to the verge of bankruptcy, financially speaking only, because of the mismanagement of the money system.
From its very inception the money system of Canada and of every other democratic country has not functioned as it should have done. The purpose of a financial system, as I see it, is to reflect the desire and the ability of the people of a nation to produce and to consume, and if it is not doing that, it is not performing its function. So long as there are idle resources and idle men, the financial system is not reflecting the ability of a country to produce. So long as there is abundance, if not actual, then potential, of goods and services on the one hand, and poverty and destitution on the other, the financial system is not reflecting the ability and the desire of the people to consume. And so long as there are any physical possibilities-I do not care which you wish to name-which are not being realized, the financial policy is not functioning as it should.
Why is it not functioning as it should? I consider that the right to create, issue and put into circulation in the first instance every single, solitary dollar and cent in the country is a crown prerogative. All money that is issued in a nation should be issued by the state. That is the most sacred of all crown prerogatives. But there are members of this house and people outside the house who state that it is not only undesirable but dangerous for the state to issue money, although the exact converse of that is the truth. The state should be the only authority within a nation to create and put into circulation all the money of the nation.

The Address-Mr. Kuhl

Abraham Lincoln made a statesmanlike utterance on this question of the state issue of money and the prerogative of the crown. He said:
Money is the creature of law, and the creation of the original issue of money should be maintained as an exclusive monopoly of the national government. Such needs can be served by issuing national currency and credit through the operation of a national banking system. The government should create, issue and circulate all the currency and credit needed to satisfy the spending power of the government and the buying power of consumers. The privilege of creating and issuing money is not only the supreme prerogative of the government but it is the government's greatest creative opportunity.
Will anyone deny that that is as it should be? Yet there are in this house men, including the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley), if not stating straightforwardly, at any rate certainly implying that it is not only unwise but dangerous for the state to issue money. I regard that as one of the most shocking circumstances in a democratic country. The state should be creating and issuing every cent of the money of this nation, but we are being told that it is unwise and dangerous to do this. This sacred prerogative of the crown, the most sacred prerogative that the crown can exercise, has been given piecemeal over a period of time to a private monopoly, and this has been carried to the point where parliament to-day has been relegated to the position of merely a pawnbroker for the private money monopoly. That is the position which the government occupies to-day.
In my opinion every person, I care not how high his position may be, or what office he may occupy, who has contributed to this state of affairs and who insists that it should be perpetuated, ought to be tried for high treason -and I mean that. I consider that giving away into the hands of a private monopoly the most sacred prerogative the crown can possess is one of the most heinous crimes that any individual or group of individuals can be guilty of, and in my opinion those persons who have been guilty of this act, regardless of who they may be, are as traitorous as any fifth columnist can be considered.
I should like to support what I have just said by a quotation from a book published by C. Barclay-Smith, entitled " Victory without Debt." He is an Australian and I recommend this book to every member of the house. Everyone should read it not only once but a hundred times; he would be a better man after reading it. At page 34 the writer says:
When public trustees:-that is, the parliament of the nation-finance government requirements by pawning the assets of the country and the
[Mr. Kuhl.l
future security of the people to the private credit monopoly, thus lowering the tenor of life of every citizen, so far from calling that kind of thing sound finance I prefer to give it its proper name-high treason.
As I have already suggested, the first reason why the financial system in Canada, the policy that is being pursued, does not do what it ought to do is the fact that the crown prerogative is exercised by a private monopoly; and the first thing that should be done is to restore to parliament and to the people of Canada this sacred prerogative. The people of Canada were led to believe that this is what the Liberal party would do if they were elected in 1935. I am quite satisfied that this is the reason why the Liberal party was elected with the majority it received in 1935. The people believed that it would restore to parliament the sacred prerogative of issuing and putting into circulation the medium of exchange. But this was not done. Why? St. James Street probably shouted " boo," and the Liberal party wilted.
I would say the second reason is that the financial policy which is in vogue in Canada does not permit what is physically possible becoming financially possible, for the reason that all money which is issued to-day originates as a debt to the banking institutions. Consequently, anyone who uses bank money-and everyone and every institution must use it-becomes perpetually in debt to the banking institutions. A debt is incurred which can never be paid. Some individuals can pay, but the nation as a whole can never get out of debt to the banking institutions, because it owes more than there is in the community with which to pay back the debt, and that is the reason why public debts, national debts, are never paid off.

Money should be created and issued in such fashion that the repayment of a debt is made a mathematical possibility. Under the present system and policy it is not. And the fact that the debts continually increase is sufficient evidence of that.
Another evil which the present policy works is that it obliges the people to pay for things not only once but twice, thrice and many more times. For instance, in public works, a project is completed, a bridge, for example, is built. The community as a whole provides everything physically needed to build that bridge, the community provides all the labour and all the material, and when that bridge is built it is actually paid for. But under the present system of financing, it is not paid for, possibly for a hundred

The Address-Mr. Kuhl
years afterwards. Financially it is paid for several times over. Physically it was paid for when it was completed.
That principle holds true in connection with war. Why should we be paying for the 1914-18 war to-day, if blood and sweat and tears constitute the only cost of a war? All the physical essentials of the 1914-18 war were met at that time, and that war was fully paid for when the war was concluded. And that holds true of the present war. The Minister of Finance has informed us that this war is being paid for as it progresses. Well, that is true; a war is paid for as it progresses. In blood, sweat and tears the cost of a war is provided from day to day as the war progresses. If that is the situation, I want to be told why there should be a debt remaining after the war is over? Why are we told after the war is over that we still have to pay for the war, if the war is being paid for while it is in progress? I should like to hear a discussion with regard to that angle.
The minister says that the government is pursuing a pay-as-you-go policy. I would call it, pay as you go now and after it is over and until you die, and your children and your grandchildren and your great grandchildren continue to pay. That is the kind of policy the government is pursuing; it is not a pay-as-you-go policy, it is a pay-a-hundred-times-as-you-go policy.
The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Claxton), in moving the address in reply, stated that Canadians will be obliged to deprive themselves until it hurts. Well, we in this corner agree to that; if sacrifices are necessary, they must be made. But because of the iniquities of the financial policy which is now being pursued, we are called upon for sacrifices which are unnecessary, and unnecessary sacrifices are iniquities.
We contend that it is possible for this country and the empire to have victory without debt. If we are paying for the war as it progresses, that can be true in a financial sense as well as in a real sense. The only cost involved in financing the war is a matter of bookkeeping, of setting up the appropriate system and conducting it while the war is in progress. All that is involved is the services of clerks and the consumption of ink and paper; outside of that there is no expense. If the cost of banking and the real costs are met during the war, we want to be told why there need be a debt after the war.
I had intended to deal with that question a little further but I see my time is gone. I should like to say something on another

Most hon. members are aware that I have interested myself particularly in Canada's constitutional question; I have spoken on it several times in this house-

In connection with the
implementation of this report I am quite in accord with the idea that we must have constitutional alterations in Canada; I have so expressed myself on several occasions. I am satisfied that such alterations are long overdue. But I frankly confess that I do not agree with the method employed, this dominion-provincial conference, to settle such a major question. The Prime Minister has represented himself in this house on many occasions as a great protagonist of democracy, but in my opinion this action to which he is resorting in an endeavour to solve a constitutional difficulty is a negation and repudiation of everything he has said on the question of democracy.
I believe the best advice that has been given to us as to the most democratic manner in which to settle this question is that given by the clerk of this house, Doctor Beauchesne, and I recommend it to every hon. member and to every province of Canada. Personally I feel that there is more democracy in one page of Doctor Beauchesne's evidence than in the whole Sirois recommendations.
I would call the Prime Minister's way of attempted settlement of the constitutional difficulty a hole-in-the-corner business, getting the premiers of the provinces or one or two representatives from each province together with the dominion cabinet, is in my view, not the way to settle such an important question. This question involves the whole people of Canada, and they should be consulted. I do not think any premier or any representative of a provincial government, without first getting authority from the people through a plebiscite, has any moral or legal right to come to any agreement as to alteration of the constitutional position in Canada. No provincial government, regardless of what majority they have, in my opinion have any
The Address-Mr. Kuhl

authority from their people to act on this question. If it is going to be done in a democratic fashion the people of each province should first be consulted before any action is taken.
I shall quote a sentence or two of Doctor Beauchesne's suggestion, and leave it at that. I agree entirely with it. Doctor Beauchesne has suggested that this all-important question should be dealt with not by a few individuals but by a constituent assembly. On page 126 of the report of the special committee on the British North America Act he is reported as saying:
I, therefore, beg to suggest an imposing constituent assembly formed of eminent men coming from all parts of Canada. Provincial conferences, attended by a few ministers meeting behind closed doors, would hardly satisfy public opinion. The debate should be published.
I believe that should be the case in connection with the consideration of this question. He continues:
I submit that a constituent assembly, chosen by the provincial legislatures and by the House of Commons, representing the main political parties and groups in proportion to the votes given at the last general elections, should meet in session at Winnipeg and discuss the situation from all its angles.
Then on page 128 this suggestion is made:
The assembly should be convened by provincial proclamations issued in each province and by a dominion proclamation in which it would be clearly stated that the minority rights now guaranteed by the British North America Act should not even be discussed.
In choosing the delegates to this constituent assembly, due regard should be given to the representation of all classes. Business men, farmers, professional men, scholars and labour men should be represented. Although the dominion would send an important delegation, the assembU should not be a dominion assembly, but rather an assembly of the provinces' representatives in consultation with the dominion.
There ought to be no government side and no official opposition in such a body, which should work on the lines of coalition. A committee consisting of the premiers and leaders of the opposition in the House of Commons and legislatures would have charge of the agenda and daily order of business which, under ordinary rules, could be adjusted daily by experienced parliamentary clerks. Speeches ought to be recorded by Hansard.
Then there is this last paragraph:
I would suggest that the assembly do not sit in Ottawa, in order that it may not have the appearance of being dominated, or even influenced, by the dominion power; and, as the western provinces are of such paramount importance in the country, I suggest the best city for the representatives to gather in would be Winnipeg.
I am heartily in accord with these suggestions. I should like to elaborate on them
a good deal more, but I have exhausted my
[Mr. Kuhi-l
time. I recommend a study of these suggestions to all members of this house and of the provincial legislatures. I believe it is only in some manner such as this that this great and all-important question can be settled in the best interests of the people of Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the course of the debate now drawing to its conclusion, many interesting things have been said. The mover of the address in reply to the speech from the throne, the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Claxton), and the seconder, the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Jutras), led the way on the first day with remarkable eloquence.
The government asks for our support in its war policy. The leader of the opposition replies that this policy is only a catch, that the war effort is insufficient and ill-managed, and he invites us to censure the government accordingly. He adds that the government is also deserving of blame for having not given more help to the farmers of Canada.
The leader of the new democracy party has found another reason for blaming the government: he wants to have Canada pay its war costs in social credit money. Let us examine his subamendment, which will be voted upon first. We have just listened to a speech advocating his theory. The money constantly recommended by hon. members in the far corner would simply consist of non-interestbearing dominion notes printed and circulated in practically unlimited quantities. Were this method feasible, the task of the Minister of Finance would be wonderfully simple. He would no longer have to find lenders nor to levy revenue to pay the thirty or forty million dollars of interest required for each billion dollars spent for war purposes. That would remove a very heavy burden from the shoulders of the taxpayers. Alas! systems that are too simple are not always the best, because they omit too many essential factors. Our national economy is necessarily conditioned by our trade relations with other countries, and we have to protect the value of our money abroad as well as at home.
At no time have our exports and imports reached their present high level. How could we, at this time, be rash enough to forsake the doctrine that is generally accepted in Great Britain and the United States as regards the issue of money? Never in our life as a nation have we been less justified than we are now in attempting risky experiments with money. Let us first win the vrar, after which we can discuss whatever experiments it might be advisable for us to try, if we are not satisfied with the monetary system then in use.

The Address,-Mr. Authier
Winning the war must be our chief concern, for let us not forget for a moment that defeat would bring about the direst consequences for Canada and the world. But, God willing, Great Britain and her sister and allied nations shall not be vanquished.
The leader of the opposition is quite unjustified in suggesting that the government of Canada have not done their duty-their full duty-and that they are merely soothing the Canadian people. One after the other, the ministers of national defence have stated to this house the activities of their departments. What criticism have the honourable members who sit on the opposition side been able to voice? A very weak one. We have been told by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) that we are spending daily three million dollars for our war effort, which is all we can afford to spend. No one has shown that those funds have not on the whole been wisely used or that there was any dishonesty in that regard. Of course, some criticism on matters of detail may have been justified, but, on the whole, necessary war expenditures have been made quite properly. I know that the government have been upbraided by some overenthusiastic members for not having sent to Europe a larger number of soldiers. Those who followed a course so obviously wrong during the last war would like to-day-in order to enhance the interests of their party-to see this government follow their example and take the road leading to conscription. We have heard to-night a speech partly devoted to the expression of such ideas. No. we are not going to make such a mistake this time. Canada shall not send overseas more men than are necessary. The British ambassador in the United States, Lord Lothian, has just stated publicly that his country had no need of reinforcements. " England definitely does not need men," he said on his arrival at New York from London. I have read that statement in the New York Times of last Sunday. Such a statement makes it unnecessary for us to look for any further rebuttal of the Conservative argument on that point.
The leader of the opposition was more fortunate in the choice of his second point, for there is indeed much unrest among the farmers in this country. However, he is wrong in suggesting that the government have done nothing to lessen it. To the members from western Canada who never cease to demand more help for the western farmers, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) easily showed that no government has ever done so much for the farmers in the prairies. I have no wish to criticize him for the help so given. Besides he did good work for the
producers of the whole country during his recent trip to Great Britain. But I would ask him to do still more for eastern farmers. I confess that we have in the province of Quebec a great many farmers whose plight is pitiful. Surely there ought to be some way of helping them. I wish to associate myself with those who have asked that these farmers be supplied at a low cost with western grain and grain products so that they may feed their cattle and produce meat more profitably. The freight rates on wheat and grain for consumption in eastern Canada should not be higher than the export rates. Such a policy would be equally fair to western and eastern Canada. Why not use the transcontinental railway from Winnipeg to Quebec, Montreal and Moncton, for the purpose that those who planned and built it had in mind?
As I said, a large number of farmers in the province of Quebec are in a sorry plight. There are, I believe, 50,000 or 60,000 settlers and farmers in Quebec who cannot obtain from their land sufficient income to provide their families with proper food, clothing and education. They are compelled to seek additional sources of income elsewhere, in the forests, the mines, the fisheries and many other occupations. Young men leave the farm at an early age to seek work in the cities where they find' themselves out of place and frequently out of employment.
WThat are the remedies? As it would take too long to go into the question in detail, I shall confine myself to generalities. A more practical and widespread system of agricultural instruction should be adopted and enforced, and more capital should be placed at the disposal of farmers capable of making profitable use of it. The dominion farm loan scheme did not produce the results it should have produced. It could be made more liberal and efficient. The progress of agriculture in the province of Quebec is a question both of education and of finance. Advance will be slow, but that is all the more reason for immediate action. While awaiting the results of a general policy, palliatives could be used, as they were used in western Canada. Why should there not be a minimum price for butter and cheese as there is for wheat? Farmers who sold their butter for 22 cents a pound all through the summer usually discover that its price to the consumer rises 25 per cent and even 35 per cent at the end of the season, as-it did this fall.
I am simply suggesting that the government set a minimum price for butter, as has been done in the case of wheat, and ensure its delivery throughout the country without any excessive profits going to the middlemen.
The Address^Mr. Authier

It would also be necessary to consider the setting of a reasonable price for all pulp-wood cut by farmers on their own land. To a great number of our settlers and would-be farmers, the sale of such wood is the only available means of livelihood. The central authority could certainly do its share in assisting them by exerting a certain pressure on our railroads whose shipping rates on this product are often much too -high. Should these measures require the cooperation of the provincial governments, it will be forthcoming. The premier of Quebec is not only a great orator, but also a very intelligent farmer, as everyone knows. He can be counted on to do his share. If the Minister of Agriculture were to accept my suggestions, he could then boast that never before has a government done as much, not only for the western farmer but for the eastern farmer as well. Our agricultural class needs and is worthy of his assistance. Once again, I know its recovery will take time and effort and a great deal of patience. Like colonization, it is apparently a deceptive undertaking because of the ceaseless difficulties and delays to be encountered, but it is a task that must nevertheless be accomplished since it is essential to maintaining a correct balance between city and country, as well as to the morale of our people and the future greatness of Canada.
I intend to vote against the opposition leader's amendment for two reasons: firstly, his leading premise is evidently without foundation and, secondly, he has suggested no remedy for the agricultural distress he mentions.
I shall continue to have faith in the statesmen who now govern this country, particularly the right hon. prime minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), who has ever shown throughout his long career a deep understanding of the realities of Canadian politics, inspired in all circumstances by a true Canadian patriotism and a great sense of social justice. Under his guidance, the administration will, I trust, take all steps required to improve the lot of our people, that of the good and the humble to whom the prime minister alluded in concluding his first address this session. The performance of this task will in no way hinder their furnishing to Great Britain the fullest measure of assistance we have promised her in this war which she is fighting so valorously and from which she will emerge triumphant and glorious.

Mr. Speakpr, upon rising to speak in this house for the first, time I should like to take this opportunity of paying a tribute to my immedi-

ate predecessor from the city of Saskatoon. The late Reverend W. G. Brown was a man of the very highest character and ability, and one who was affectionately regarded by all those with whom he came in contact, regardless of their political affiliations. He came to this house from no selfish motive, for no reasons of self-advancement, but purely for the purpose of speaking on behalf of those people for whom he had laboured all the days of his life, men and women in destitute and necessitous circumstances. His passing was a great blow to the city from which I come and to this country which he loved so well.
This evening I wish to discuss two matters relating to western economy. I am not a farmer and I do not have that detailed knowledge of farming which can be acquired only by those actually engaged in that occupation, but I did spend some part of my youth on the farm. I am also a resident of the city of Saskatoon, -which is the hub of the greatest hard wheat growing country in the world, and I know how vital the production and sale of our wheat are not only to the farmers themselves but to those residing in cities such as the one from which I come. I know how very much concerned we are in the west over the situation that exists out there at the present time. Only a very small fringe of the population of my city is actually engaged in farming, some 1,500 out of about 43,000 people, but every man and woman in my constituency is materially interested either directly or indirectly in agriculture and particularly in wheat and the price of it. The whole economy of my constituency, indeed of my province, depends upon the production of wheat and the money that, is obtained for it.
It is bad enough to have to exist in an economy that is dependent upon a price of 70 cents for No. 1 northern at Fort William, which means about 52 cents in my district. That is a price which it is generally conceded is not sufficient to keep the farmer on the land as an efficient producer. I was pleased indeed, as I am sure many other members were, to hear the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) make that admission the other day when he stated in the house:
It is generally admitted that 70 cents advance at Fort William, which nets the farmer about 50 cents a bushel, does not cover his total costs of production and therefore does not maintain him as a contented producer.
I like those words, "contented producer," because I am convinced that you cannot have an efficient producer unless you have one that is at least reasonably contented. May I

The Address-Mr. Bence
express the hope that the hon. Minister of Agriculture will continue to impress that fact upon the house and upon the government of which he is a member?
It is bad enough, as I have said, to have to exist in an economy based on wheat at that price, but it is a very sorry situation indeed when we cannot obtain even that amount of money for our product. I have been listening and watching carefully to leam what statements would be made by the government in connection with an advance on wheat stored on the farm. The two ministers who were mainly concerned with this matter after the house adjourned last August, the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon), have both addressed the house within the last week or so. The Minister of Agriculture had nothing to say about an advance on wheat stored on the farm, and the Minister of Trade and Commerce very little indeed. He contented himself, as I recall it, with stating that because the banks felt it was not a good risk, the government had to drop the matter.
The opinion was general throughout this land last August and September that the question of making an advance payment on wheat stored on the farm had already been settled. Indeed, some of us were taken to task because it was claimed that we were insisting upon something being considered which had already been decided upon. In proof of that fact I should like to quote briefly from an editorial in the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix of August 31, 1940, as follows:
There has been a great deal of ineffective talk about the problem, a considerable effort to make use of it for political purposes and considerable demanding of things already assured.
Thus, it is tremendously important that advances be made on the wheat left on farms. That has been recognized by everyone concerned from the start. It requires no emphasis. But away back in July Ottawa had already made the decision to make such advances. Several ministers announced it in the House of Commons and have repeated it since. Yet a vast amount of energy has been used up demanding that which was already decided.
That this feeling was not restricted to Saskatoon and to Saskatchewan is evidenced by a statement appearing in Canadian Finance of September 18, 1940, from which I quote as follows:
But there have been definite statements from Ottawa that money is to be advanced to farmers on grain held in farm storage and it is generally assumed that the advances will be handled by the wheat board.
In addition to that, the Minister of Trade and Commerce on several occasions indicated most strongly that an advance would be made
and that the only question was as to the exact method of working it out. As a result of the statements that were made and of the impression at least that was given, credit was granted in many cases by the merchants, but in many other instances that was impossible because the many years of drought and low prices had left the merchants of Saskatchewan in a position where they could not advance the credit they would like to have done.
I have received a letter written on behalf of the fuel merchants of western Canada pointing out to me that there were many farmers who would be in need of the delivery of coal but who could not purchase it because all the money they had received from the sale of their quota was required to pay immediate expenses-and that was after the quota had been raised to its present level. I quote from that letter, dated September 27, 1940, as follows:
In the past it has been the practice for a farmer to bring in a load of grain and take out a load of coal-taking delivery from the car and thus saving unloading expense and perhaps getting a better quality of coal; this year, however, he has to utilize the money received from the little grain he can sell for payment of current expenses and this leaves him with little or nothing with which to purchase his fuel requirements. Cold weather will soon be upon us and these people will be looking for fuel; in nine cases out of ten the farmer will have utilized his full quota and he will, therefore, be unable to follow the practice of former years-that of selling wheat and taking out coal-and there are no coal dealers in western Canada prepared to sell fuel to the farmer without money, as their experience in this connection has been too sad over the past years.
Because of the fact that advances were not made a great deal of hardship resulted not only for the farmers but for merchants both rural, and urban, and a trade paralysis resulted which never should have been allowed to arise.
The history of what happened after parliament adjourned last August would appear to be that the Minister of Trade and Commerce stayed in Ottawa for several weeks after the date he had intended to go on his holidays, to give this matter the grave consideration which it deserved. He received representations from all parts of western Canada-the prairies in any event-and the Bracken committee was called together, under the convenership of Premier John Bracken of Manitoba, and had a conference with the government and the wheat board. But the result of these representations and of the conference was a very sad one indeed as far as the western farmers and western merchants generally were concerned.
I believe that we should have from the Minister of Trade and Commerce a fuller

Moreover, the suggestion has been made in this house, and at least in one newspaper that I noticed, that women will probably have to be called to assist in manufacturing work. I realize that there is one in far eastern Canada, but I am only discussing the question from the point of view of the western provinces. It is true that the relief problem in the prairie provinces was not as great this summer as it had been in many of the years before. It was not as great this fall, either, but there are still many people on relief in Saskatoon, and it is anticipated that the number will be considerably augmented in the next few months, because the work they have been doing has been completed or nearly completed. They have been building air ports and barracks and similar construction, but after the work is done there is nothing further for them to do and they must go back on relief. These works in themselves will not give employment except to the army and navy, and unless we do something to build factories or industrial concerns, which will in themselves provide employment, we shall always have a problem on the western prairies.
Besides relief, there is a tremendous labour force on the farms, and a part of the farmer's product will not be wanted and he will have to be supported by the state either directly or indirectly. This anomaly of a great labour shortage in one part of the country and a great force of labour in another, idle and supported in large part from public funds, should not be allowed to continue without some strenuous efforts being made to correct it.
The Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) explained the other day that the reason why so many of the industries for war purposes were being concentrated in Ontario and Quebec was that hydro-electric power made for low cost of production. He did not say that it was essential for efficient work; he did not say that the work could not be done in the west and in other parts of Canada just as quickly and efficiently as in Ontario and Quebec. The point he stressed was that it could be done more cheaply in these two provinces. Speaking to this house last May he said:
I am greatly interested in just one thing, and that is getting the best material available in the shortest time and at the lowest price.
In the house the other day he said that he wished to conduct his department as he would

a business concern. These are laudable sentiments and in a large measure we can all agree with them. One thing he seems to have forgotten is the fact that this is an effort by the whole of Canada and that the whole of Canada wishes to participate in providing essential war materials. I would suggest to him that if we could work out some scheme which, although possibly it would cost the department more money now, would in the long run save money for Canada, it would be a good thing.
We should look at the matter from a much broader point of view, and my suggestion is that at the risk of costing a little more now, so long as speed is not impaired, and so long as the war effort is not impeded, we should make a strenuous effort through the medium of war industry to divert the great labour force in western Canada and in other parts of the country outside Ontario and Quebec, at least in part, from their present occupations into essential war industries. In my own city war work on a smaller scale could be done now, but it may be that it could not be done at a price which would compete with that available in eastern Canada. There is a growing demand in the west to transfer labour from grain production to necessary war work. To bonus nonproduction, idleness or useless overproduction is economically unsound. We must have a diversified economy throughout our country, not only to assist in the war work but for post-war purposes.
There is an opportunity before us which we must not miss. If we do not take advantage of it now, we shall probably never have it again. The self-sufficiency which the European nations attained after the first great war, and the difficulty of getting a remunerative price for wheat in peace time, should be warning to us to take advantage of this opportunity when we have it. If we plan carefully and establish industries in other parts of Canada-and as I said I am not by any means confining myself to the prairies-in the long run we shall be able to save a great deal of money and establish the economic structure of this dominion on a sound basis. It is imperative that we do everything in our power to iron out the economic sectionalism which besets this country like a plague.
In conclusion I wish to associate myself most strongly and sincerely with those who have raised their voices in this house on behalf of the soldiers with regard to the request for free transportation. The Associate Minister of National Defence (Mr. Power) indicated I believe this afternoon that nothing was going to be done in this regard as far as

Christmas leave is concerned. Well, I trust the government will not make that final. In any event I make this plea, that they do not allow any soldier, sailor or airman to go overseas without first having an opportunity to go and see his loved ones.
